15rvqzi.content: Автомобиль, привезенный из-за рубежа и числящийся в розыскной базе Интерпола, вовсе не обязательно терять. Адвокат Тимур Чанышев объяснил: такую машину реально оставить за собой и поставить на учет в РФ. Опирается он на позицию Верховного суда – сам факт розыска не является безусловным основанием для отказа в регистрации.Неприятнее всего, когда о проблеме узнаешь уже после покупки. Первым делом в таком случае нужен письменный отказ ГИБДД. Дальше имеет смысл выяснить причины розыска и запросить документы о хищении. Доказательств не хватает? Тогда ограничения оспариваются в суде. Правда, если хищение подтвердится, собственник вправе истребовать авто даже у добросовестного покупателя.Чтобы не попасть в такую историю, Чанышев советует проверять VIN по российским и международным базам, изучать историю владения и прописывать в договоре гарантии продавца об отсутствии розыска.Ранее «За рулем» рассказывал, что Минфин направит на льготный автолизинг 26 млрд руб. за два года. gh-1460793150.title: GitHub - Berny23/slingshot-animals-recomp: Unofficial static recompilation of Rovio's old Angry Birds games. Classic, Seasons, Rio, Space, Star Wars, Star Wars 2, Stella.
gh-1460793150.content:
Unofficial static recompilation of Rovio's old Android Angry Birds games. Each game's native ARM library is translated to C++ and runs natively on Linux, Windows, macOS and 64-bit Android, without an emulator.
ImportantNo game files are included or linked here. You need your own legally obtained copy of each game.
The game is built locally on your device, for your personal use only.

Install

Download Slingshot Builder for your system from the releases (Linux AppImage, Windows exe, macOS app).
Open it, drop the APK of a supported version onto the window and press Build & Install.

The game then appears in your system as a separate app. For Android, you can chose to build an APK file and copy it onto your phone, or install the app via ADB directly on a connected phone (recommended for advanced users).

Linux: Just run the AppImage.
Windows: As the builder is not signed, SmartScreen may warn you, which is normal. Just click More info → Run anyway.
MacOS: Open the builder with right-click → Open the first time. It needs Apple's Command Line Tools and offers to install them.

To uninstall the games on Linux, just delete them under ~/.local/lib/slingshot-animals-recomp/ and their menu entries at ~/.local/share/applications/slingshot-<id>.desktop.
Features

Runs the original game logic, graphics, sound and text rendering natively
Plays offline: Rovio's online services, ads and in-app purchases are stubbed
Mouse or touch screen as on Android, Esc is the Back key
Language follows the system locale or --locale
Mods for keyboard and gamepad play, offline versions of online features and more, see below

Mods
All mods are on by default. In the builder, Advanced chooses which ones a game starts with; --no-mod <name> turns one off for a single start.

Mod
Games
Description

mouse-wheel
all
Mouse wheel zooms in levels and scrolls menus

keyboard
all
Play with the keyboard: hold Space, aim with W A S D or arrows, release to shoot, Space again for the bird's ability; arrows move the camera, + / - zoom, R restarts, P pauses, Enter continues

gamepad-pointer
all
Play with a gamepad: the left stick moves a cursor (right stick slowly), A taps, triggers zoom, B is Back

tap-to-skip
all
Tap to skip the wait at the end of a level

fullscreen
all
F11 toggles fullscreen

hide-dead-services
all
Hides buttons and messages of discontinued online services

offline-shop
all
Everything sold for real money can be earned by playing

game-statistics
all
Statistics page with achievements and progress to 100 %

offline-league
Classic
Mighty League without servers

offline-tournament
Seasons
Pig Challenge without servers: weeks open one after another, all weeks replayable after the last

composite-audio
Star Wars, Star Wars II
Plays the menu music and power-up sounds again

offline-assets
Star Wars II
Starts without the download server (see below)

audio-quality
Stella
Stereo sound at 24 kHz, better than on Android

seasonal-menu
Seasons
The main menu shows a random episode of the current season (Halloween, Christmas, ...). --mod-option seasonal-menu.season=<name> picks one

offline-clock
Star Wars II
Timed features use the device's clock

missing-translations
Rio
Translates texts the game shows only in English

samsung-level
Space, Star Wars II
Content once given only to Samsung devices is open everywhere

Supported versions
APKs with the armeabi-v7a library:

The build checks each library's SHA-256.
Star Wars II downloads its sounds and theme images from a server that is gone; without them it plays silence and draws simplified backgrounds. For the originals, copy files/assets_service/ from a device installation (/data/data/com.rovio.angrybirdsstarwarsii.ads/) into the game's save folder, on Linux:
~/.local/share/slingshot-animals-recomp/starwars2/internal/files/assets_service/
├── 16000hz-16bit-mono/ music/ and sfx/ (*.mp3)
└── images/ android/ (THEME_*.pvr, THEME_*.dat)

Build
Needs CMake 3.28, Ninja or Make and a C++20 compiler. On Linux also capstone, SDL3, FreeType, HarfBuzz, liblzma and zlib; elsewhere these are downloaded and built (-DSLINGSHOT_SYSTEM_DEPS=OFF does the same on Linux).
cmake -S . -B build -DGAME_APKS="/path/to/angrybirds.apk;/path/to/angrybirdsrio.apk"
cmake --build build

Each APK is matched to its game by the library and extracted to build/games/<id>/; every game gets its own executable build/bin/slingshot-<id>. Recompiling a game needs up to 1.5 GB of memory, so games are recompiled one at a time. Build options:

-DSLINGSHOT_DEFAULT_MODS=all|none|<list>: mods enabled by default, e.g. "hide-dead-services;offline-shop"
-DSLINGSHOT_MODS=OFF: build without mods

Cross builds use the recompiler built for this machine (-DSLINGSHOT_HOST_TOOLS=build/host-tools):

Windows: -DCMAKE_TOOLCHAIN_FILE=cmake/toolchains/llvm-mingw.cmake -DLLVM_MINGW=<llvm-mingw>
Android: -DCMAKE_TOOLCHAIN_FILE=<ndk>/build/cmake/android.toolchain.cmake -DANDROID_ABI=arm64-v8a -DANDROID_PLATFORM=android-24 -DSLINGSHOT_ANDROID_SDK=<sdk> -DSLINGSHOT_JDK=<jdk> builds bin/slingshot-<id>.apk, signed with -DSLINGSHOT_ANDROID_KEYSTORE (created if missing; updates need the same key)

The builder app is a separate project: cmake -S tools/builder -B build-builder (Qt 6.5 or newer). It builds in KDE's Breeze style and uses it everywhere; -DSLINGSHOT_BUILDER_BREEZE=OFF keeps Qt's platform styles.
Run
build/bin/slingshot-<id> [options] [game-dir]

Option
Description

--list-mods
List the mods

--mod <name>
Enable only the given mods (repeatable), like SLINGSHOT_MODS=a,b

--no-mod <name>
Disable a mod

--no-mods
Original game without mods

--mod-option <mod>.<key>=<value>
A setting for a mod (repeatable), see the mod table

--locale <ll_CC>
Game language, e.g. de_DE

--dump-scripts <dir>
Write the game's scripts and configs out decrypted

Saves are in ~/.local/share/slingshot-animals-recomp/<id>/ (or $XDG_DATA_HOME) on Linux, %APPDATA%\slingshot-animals-recomp\<id>\ on Windows and ~/Library/Application Support/slingshot-animals-recomp/<id>/ on macOS; on Android they stay in the app's storage until it is uninstalled. They are encrypted by the game; copy the folder while the game is not running to back them up.
Modding
The game logic is Lua 5.1 bytecode (4-byte numbers), the configs are JSON. In the APK both are encrypted and compressed; the games read plain scripts too:

build/bin/slingshot-<id> --dump-scripts ~/ab-scripts writes the scripts (data/**/*.lua) and JSON files in the layout of assets/, decrypted by the game's own code. Classic also writes config.json and data/config/*.zip. A script that is a 7z archive is written as <name>.7z where the game's loader for it is not hooked.
Replace a script in build/games/<id>/assets/ with an edited one, as Lua source or bytecode. Classic and Seasons take plain JSON files and configs too.

Sprite sheet descriptions (*.sheet.json, *.compo.json) are dumped for reference but cannot be replaced yet. The built-in mods patch scripts in memory, see docs/ARCHITECTURE.md.
Note
This project does not include any original game files. You need your own copies of the APKs. It is not affiliated with or endorsed by Rovio; Angry Birds is a trademark of Rovio Entertainment.

gh-1167940088.title: GitHub - jasonij/JetSetRusty: Jet Set Willy (1984) — 100% Rust/SDL3, ported from C just for fun
gh-1167940088.content:
Some rando on the internet is porting fawtytoo's C version of JetSetWilly into
Rust. This is that port.
A Rust port of Jet Set Willy, the 1984 ZX Spectrum game by Matthew Smith
(Software Projects). It is ported from
fawtytoo/JetSetWilly, Steve Clark's
C/SDL2 reimplementation. The game is now 100% Rust, with no C compiled, and
gameplay is meant to be identical to the C version.
The reference implementation in C lives surprisingly in the
reference/c-original/ — directory. More commits have
been made to the original since I started this and I haven't ported them over
quite yet.
Note the zlib LICENCE (clause 2) requires altered versions to
be plainly marked as such. So, this is a modified port, not the original
software (see Licence below), although the C original in included for
reference (in a directory by that very name).
You can see the original README.md here

What carries over from the C version
These are all features of fawtytoo's version, preserved in the port:

Gameplay identical to the original, minus a few original bugs that were
fixed, such as landing at the end of a jump into a solid wall.
Per-pixel colouring, so there is no colour clash, with a 16-colour palette.
Two replacement character-set fonts, one small and one large.
Polyphonic title and in-game music, plus approximate original sound
effects with stereo panning. All sound comes from a square-wave synth
for that retro "beepy" sound.

Controls

Key
Action

← / →
Walk

Space
Jump

Tab or Pause
Pause

Alt
Music on/off

Esc
Quit to title

Cheat mode
Type the cheat code just like in the original. Once it's active, hold a level
key and press Enter: 1–0 select levels 1–10, A–T select levels 11–30,
and holding Shift moves those to 31–60. See ROOMS.md for the
full room list.
Copy protection
The original shipped with a "code card" you had to consult after loading. To
skip entering codes, press any key during the "JetSet Willy Loading" sequence.

Building
You need a Rust toolchain (edition 2024), a C compiler, and cmake. SDL3 is
built from source by the sdl3 crate and linked statically, so no system SDL
package is required:
sudo apt install build-essential cmake # Debian/Ubuntu
cargo run --release # the first build compiles SDL3 itself; takes a few minutes
Only Linux is tested at the moment.
Fresh clones need git config core.hooksPath .githooks once to enable the
repo's hooks — pre-commit runs cargo build and blocks the commit if the
build fails.

The original C
The C implementation this was ported from is kept, buildable, in
reference/c-original/. It includes upstream's
original README, and
PROVENANCE.md explains where it came
from. Cargo does not compile it.
Licence
zlib licence; see LICENCE. Copyright © 2021–2026 Steve Clark and
© 1984 Matthew Smith (Software Projects). In keeping with the licence, this is
an altered version: a Rust port, not the original software.

50q7gf.title: How enhanced rock weathering can speed up carbon capture
50q7gf.content:
UC Davis postdoctoral scholar Jaeeun Sohng and UC Davis professor of earth and planetary sciences Isabel Montañez stand inside a sampling station at the Sierra Foothill Research and Extension Center, where they're studying the decarbonization effects of adding crushed rock to soil. Credit: Gregory Urquiaga/UC Davis

Water flooded the pasture, spilling from an irrigation pipe tucked alongside a hill at the Sierra Foothill Research and Extension Center, a University of California research facility located about 20 miles (32 kilometers) east of Yuba City. For more than three hours, starting at 6 a.m. this summer day, the water had seeped into the soils beneath the yellow-green grass, spreading to various depths while flowing downslope toward its destination.

Downhill, Jaeeun Sohng donned rubber gloves and grabbed a sampling bottle. She stood inside an open-air shed built inside a trench cut into the hillside. Sohng knelt and collected water from one of the four spouts releasing the liquid after it had flowed down through the soil. A staccato-like clacking sound punctuated the white noise of running water.
"We are trying to be very particular about sampling," said Sohng, a postdoctoral scholar at the UC Davis Institute of the Environment. "We want to capture the water sample before it interacts with the atmosphere too much. For us, it's vital to understand the chemistry of the water as it exists in the soil."
Sohng is part of the California Collaborative for Natural Climate Change Solutions, a UC Davis interdisciplinary research team studying the efficacy of enhanced rock weathering, one of Earth's most powerful and ancient natural chemical reactions. For billions of years, the Earth's climate has been regulated by the ebbs and flows of this process, in which excess carbon dioxide in the atmosphere is soaked up by the natural breakdown of silicate rocks around the planet.

Sohng collects water from one of the four spouts releasing the liquid after it's traveled downslope through the soil. Credit: Gregory Urquiaga/UC Davis

But our current climate moment is a unique one. Since the Industrial Revolution, the planet's atmospheric carbon dioxide levels have increased exponentially, hitting levels not seen in nearly 14 million years. Humanity's input of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere has outpaced the climatic benefits of the planet's natural rock weathering process.

With current carbon dioxide levels hovering around 425 parts per million, more than 50% higher than preindustrial levels, researchers are interested in enhancing the rock weathering process as part of a mosaic of solutions to help humanity navigate climate change.
"We're taking one of nature's most powerful and longest-lived chemical reactions and trying to take a geoengineered approach to it," said Isabel Montañez, a professor in the Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences. "Why can't we speed up this process artificially by applying the very rock that does this chemical reaction so efficiently to agricultural lands? We can do this by using what is considered a waste product for the mining industry: rock dust."
Montañez and Toby O'Geen, a professor in the Department of Land, Air and Water Resources, are leading a multiyear, comprehensive study to quantify the benefits of applying pulverized basalt rocks to agricultural fields. This not only has the potential to benefit decarbonization efforts, but it could also improve the nutrient content of the soil, a boon for healthier crop production.

UC Davis professor of earth and planetary sciences Isabel Montañez holds sampling bottles as she stands in her research team's field site at the Sierra Foothill Research and Extension Center. Credit: Gregory Urquiaga/UC Davis

How does enhanced rock weathering work?
The science behind enhanced rock weathering is fairly straightforward. When rain falls and mixes with carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, it creates carbonic acid, an important driver of the global carbon cycle. Due to its acidity, carbonic acid dissolves rock. This chemical interaction allows for the capture of excess carbon, which is soaked up by soil and groundwater.

"Naturally, this is just a very slow process that can take hundreds of thousands of years to have any effect on the carbon dioxide in the atmosphere," Montañez said. "But importantly, it's what made for a habitable planet."
When geochemists look at the geological record, they can pinpoint times in Earth's history when rock weathering led to lower carbon dioxide levels in the atmosphere and thus a cooler climate. For example, when the Himalayas formed tens of millions of years ago, the planet "was weathering like mad," as Montañez put it.

Left to right, Seth Whiteaker, Radomir Schmidt and Isabel Montañez discuss the efficacy of enhanced rock weathering as part of the world's efforts to capture excess carbon from the atmosphere. Credit: Gregory Urquiaga/UC Davis

At the global scale, rock weathering allowed for the formation of an environment that was eventually favorable to humanity. But as carbon dioxide emissions increased, both naturally and from human activity, that trend has reversed, leading to our precarious climate conditions.
"Even if we went fully to green energy, we have to be removing carbon dioxide from the atmosphere because there is legacy carbon dioxide residing in the atmosphere that we must remove to get to net zero carbon targets," said Montañez. "We have no choice."
Realizing this, researchers around the globe have been exploring the climatic and agricultural benefits of enhanced rock weathering. Pulverizing basalt rocks to a fine sand and applying it to agricultural lands could speed up the decarbonization process.
"The estimates are that 37% of Earth's landscape has agricultural or ranch land that could do this successfully," Montañez said. "If that were the case, the estimates are it could bring down about 1 to 5 billion tons (0.9 billion to 4.5 billion metric tons) of carbon dioxide per year."
"What enhanced rock weathering is doing is taking that carbonic acid and turning it into bicarbonate," explained Seth Whiteaker, a doctoral student who is co-advised by Montañez and O'Geen. "That means that at the end, we've got carbon that stays in the water longer and either precipitates in the soil, essentially forming limestone in soils, or it gets washed out to the ocean and remains sequestered for thousands of years."

Water spills from an irrigation pipe tucked alongside a hill at the Sierra Foothill Research and Extension Center, soaking an experimental field that's been layered with pulverized basalt rocks. Credit: Gregory Urquiaga/UC Davis

The complexity of soils: A proving ground for foundational science
Some companies have embraced the potential of enhanced rock weathering. In 2025 and 2026, Microsoft and Google were among corporations that invested hundreds of millions of dollars into startups researching the process. Montañez herself has been an unpaid adviser for Microsoft and worked with the company to develop criteria for large-scale deployment.
While the idea of applying pulverized rock to agricultural lands sounds simple, there are many unknowns about its efficacy.
"There's just not enough science to show how, where and why this works best," O'Geen said. "If we can discover those things, then we have a much stronger case for convincing people that this practice is not only good for the environment, but it might actually benefit the bottom line for farmers by making the soils healthier."

UC Davis doctoral student Seth Whiteaker crouches in the team's experimental field site as he explains the nuances of their enhanced rock weathering research. Credit: Gregory Urquiaga/UC Davis

"The money is ahead of the science," O'Geen added. "We're not able to monetize correctly because we don't understand the magnitudes of carbon sequestration."
That's why O'Geen and Montañez have partnered on their research. Montañez brings the geochemical expertise while O'Geen is an expert in soil sciences. For close to two years, their field site at the Sierra Foothill Research and Extension Center has acted as an enhanced rock weathering proving ground, with the goal of detecting the rate of weathering and learning how soils influence the movement of carbon through Earth's water system.

"Soils are alive," explained O'Geen. "We think of it as brown, crumbly stuff on the surface, but they are structured, they are layered, they have a variety of colors, they are breathing, they are replicating. In a teaspoon of soil, there are over 5 billion organisms."
All that complexity influences the efficacy of the enhanced rock weathering process. In their experimental pastures, the team has spread pulverized basalt rock across the top layer of soil. Every two weeks, they flush the field with irrigation water. Every eighth week, they take solid soil and soil water samples.
Radomir Schmidt, a UC Davis project scientist, manages the research team's field site at the Sierra Foothill Research and Extension Center. Schmidt was the person who started irrigating the team's field site at 6 a.m. on their sampling day. As he drove around on a four-wheeler, he explained the thought process behind the experimental setup.
Water, whether from irrigation or rainfall, is essential for the chemical reactions of weathering. The water seeps into the soils, which soak up the liquid like a giant sponge. Once the soils reach a certain threshold, they release the water, leaking it downslope. That leaked water picks up subtle telltale signs of weathering. The water is then sampled at the foot of the hill in a dugout trench that looks like an open-air shed. The various spouts from where the water is collected correlate to soil layers at different depths.
On sampling day, Sohng and other members of the research team logged water flow rates and collected samples, which will be analyzed for their carbon, nutrient and isotope contents later in a lab. The data is helping the team understand how enhanced rock weathering changes soil-water chemistry and carbon dynamics, providing indicators of how quickly the rock powder is weathering and how much carbon could potentially travel through waterways to the ocean for long-term sequestration.

Quantifying carbon benefits: A slew of questions
While preliminary results look promising, the team also is interested in understanding the carbon costs of the enhanced rock weathering process.
"There's a balance between how much energy you use getting the rock out of the ground, crushing it, getting it out into the field and then how much carbon it takes up," said Schmidt. "Is this actually going to make a difference? Or are you producing more greenhouse gases in the process of getting the rock to the field?"
To help answer these questions, Whiteaker developed an online decision support tool that aggregates information from 4,000 mines across the United States. The tool shows how far you can transport pulverized rock material while still getting a carbon benefit.
"If you're trucking heavy things around, you're burning fuel and that has a carbon impact," Whiteaker said. "For this to really work from the carbon perspective, we need industry-wide coordination on standards to make sure that the rocks that we're spreading are of high quality and that there is coordination around how we're moving things."
Essentially, the tool maps out mines across the United States, estimates how quickly the mineral material from those mines could weather and then maps the transportation mechanisms—including road, rail and barge—to get that pulverized material to land.
"If you leverage all three, there's actually a surprising amount of the United States that is accessible to be able to get a carbon benefit," O'Geen said.

Interdisciplinary science amid an uncertain future
Montañez, O'Geen and their fellow researchers are hard at work quantifying the benefits of enhanced rock weathering, but hurdles to the science have emerged. In 2025, the team was informed that it had lost its federal funding for the project. O'Geen said federal support will dry up around the fall or winter of 2027. Some of that financial gap has been filled by generous philanthropic support.
"We're trying to do everything we can to keep it going so that we can continue this work," he said. "I'm hoping to keep it open as long as we can."
The importance of the science can't be overstated. Enhanced rock weathering is not only a crucial piece of the climate solution puzzle, but it's also a process that requires interdisciplinary and sustained research to understand. Making an impact requires the concerted effort of geochemists, soil experts and agricultural scientists and buy-in from farmers and corporations.
"This kind of work will never be successful unless you bring in people from truly different walks of academia," Montañez said.

Who's behind this story?

Lisa Lock

BA art history, MA material culture. Former museum editor, paramedic, and transplant coordinator. Editing for Science X since 2021.

Full profile →

Andrew Zinin

Master's in physics with research experience. Long-time science news enthusiast. Plays key role in Science X's editorial success.

gh-1428228424.content:
YW4 Recomp

Yo-kai Watch 4++, recompiled for PC.

4K · Ultrawide 21:9 / 32:9 · PCSS soft shadows · TAA / SMAA · ×16 texture filtering · Xbox, PlayStation and Joy-Cons

A fan static recompilation of the Nintendo Switch game (update 2.2.0), in the style of N64Recomp: the game's code is translated into a native Windows program.

The title screen, recompiled and running natively on Windows (Vulkan, 30 frames/s).

ImportantBuilt with AI. Claude (Anthropic's model, used through Claude Code) wrote most of this repository: the
recompiler, the runtime, the reverse engineering notes and these docs. A human decides what to work on, plays and
tests every build, compares it against the real game and reviews the changes. It is a personal fan project that
happens to be public. If AI-written code is not something you want to use or read, feel free to pass on it; if you
do run it, that is your call.

NotePlatforms:

Windows - x86-64, Vulkan graphics backend (this is what is built and tested): NVIDIA RTX, and AMD Radeon
(decision 0059): a Ryzen 5 7530U laptop's integrated graphics
runs it at about 35-40 frames/s at native resolution, where the Eden emulator gets 22-30
Linux - x86-64, Vulkan: works. Tester ouni666 plays it on AOSC OS (KDE Plasma, Wayland) with an AMD RX 6600 XT at
about 110-120 frames/s, the GPU at full load, with sound and controls working. The launcher runs on Linux too, as
an AppImage (decision 0071). FSR and DLSS upscaling and FSR frame
generation are built for Linux (decision 0073), not yet tried on a real
Linux GPU; DLSS frame generation and Reflex are Windows only

NoteBring your own game. Nothing from the game is in this repository. You need files from your own copy of
Yo-kai Watch 4++ with the last update, 2.2.0. Getting those files is up to you and is not covered here.

Status
Tip1.5.0 is out (beta): get the launcher, it installs the game and keeps it up to date.
Download it here, then see How to play.

Playable, but not finished. Nobody has played the game from start to finish yet.

Tested: from boot through the start of a new game (the opening, the Amano house and the town), and from
late-game saves: towns at night, the bamboo forest, the Yo-kai World and battles.
Not tested: most of the story in between. Expect missing effects and crashes in places nobody has reached.
Found a bug? Use Report a bug in the launcher or in the game's overlay.

More: what is known to be missing or wrong · how it got here, step by step
How to play
Download the launcher: on Windows the installer, or
the portable zip, which is the same app with no installer; on Linux the AppImage.
It takes your game files (NSP, XCI or extracted folders), checks them, builds the game on your PC once (about 10 to
15 minutes) and starts it. After that it opens on Play, with what's new, your screenshots, mods, DLC, saves and
logs. Its theme is synced with the in-game overlay's, and game updates come through it. Every step and screen is on
the launcher's page. To work on the code,
build from source.

The launcher building the game (video)

If you see graphical glitches
If something looks wrong, like broken or flickering shadows, change the game's renderer setting:

Open the overlay with Escape, then go to Settings and open Advanced.
Open the Developer options page at the end of Advanced.
Set SHADOW PASS from CUSTOM to GAME.

This makes the game draw the shadows with its own renderer instead of ours. It will lower performance, so
expect a lower frame rate. If the glitch is still there, try G-BUFFER the same way. Set the options back to
CUSTOM if the game runs too slowly.
Why not just use an emulator?
Switch emulators already run Yo-kai Watch 4++ at full speed on a good PC. This project aims further:
better rendering, better graphics and better performance than the Switch version (see Goals).
An emulator can't do most of this. It imitates the console and plays the game's GPU commands as they are, so the
game still decides its shadow quality, its 16:9 UI, its 30 frames/s and its effects. Here the game's renderer is
being replaced with our own, so those become ours to change: higher resolution, sharper textures, bigger and soft
shadows, anti-aliasing that leaves the UI sharp (TAA included) and ultrawide are already in, as are 60 frames/s and
above, upscaling with NVIDIA DLSS or AMD FSR (the world drawn smaller and rebuilt at full size, the menus kept
sharp) and frame generation with either (a frame made between each two of the game's).
A town street, same spot: the game's shadows (1024 map, no PCSS) against ours (4096 map, PCSS ×2). The
characters' shadows keep their shape, and the tree shade on the pavement is soft:

It is also lighter to run. The same busy street on the same laptop (docs/baseline.md,
2026-10-22), both at the game's own settings (1600×900, 30 frames/s, every improvement of this project off), so
the two do the same work:

Emulator (Eden)
This project

CPU
210% of one core
111%

Memory
~7 GB
3.9 GB

GPU
30%
33%

Memory: Eden's is private + mapped (the emulated console's RAM is mapped memory, which Task Manager's Memory
column leaves out: it shows about 1.3 GB for Eden and 2.8 GB for this project). Ours is everything the game has
committed.
On an ASUS Zenbook (Ryzen 5 7530U, integrated Radeon graphics): about 35-40 frames/s here, 22-30 in Eden (more on the site's Showcases page).

YW4 Recomp vs Eden on the Zenbook (video)

Features
What the PC version adds to the Switch game. Open an entry for details, pictures and measurements; more in docs/graphics.md.
Compare them with before/after sliders → (the project's site: ilfforever.github.io/YW4Recomp)
Graphics

Resolution: up to 4K, menus and text at the same size
The 3D world at 1600×900 (the Switch's), 1920×1080, 2560×1440 or 3840×2160; the menus and text are drawn at the same size on top. About 90+ frames/s at 4K on an RTX 4070 laptop with the other features off; with upscaling (under Performance) higher.

Aspect ratio: 16:10, 21:9 and 32:9, the UI kept 16:9 in the middle
16:9 (the Switch's), 16:10, 21:9 and 32:9. Below, 21:9 in the schoolyard: the world goes on at
the sides; the minimap and button hints stay where they are on the Switch.

Exploring, cutscenes and battles all work at the wider ratios. 21:9 at 4K height (5120×2160), from play:

Layers over the whole screen, like the dimming behind a dialog and the loading screen's black, cover the full
width; pictures made for 16:9 (the copyright notice, movies, the dungeon map's backdrop) stay 16:9 in the middle
with black bars, and the town's fast-travel map shows more of the town at the sides. At 4K ultrawide there are
occasional stutters in heavy scenes; more optimization is planned (known issues).
Menus, maps and battles at 21:9 (the dialog at 2133×900, the rest at 5120×2160):

Shadow map size: up to 4096, for sharper shadow edges
A bigger shadow map gives sharper, more detailed shadow edges, most visibly on shadows far from
the camera. The bamboo forest, PCSS off:

Soft shadows (PCSS): sharp where a shadow touches its caster, softer farther away
PCSS (percentage-closer soft shadows) makes shadows behave more like real ones. It softens a shadow by how far it
is from what casts it:

Close shadows stay sharp: where a shadow touches its caster (feet, poles, the base of a wall).
Farther shadows get softer: the farther the caster is from the ground, the softer the edge, so tree canopies
become soft dappled shade instead of a field of hard dots.
Less shimmering: hard edges flicker as the camera moves; softer ones spread that out, so distant shadows
shimmer much less.

Contact shadows: the small shadows the shadow map is too coarse for
The shadow map can't see small, close detail. Contact shadows fill it in from the picture itself: a short ray from
each point toward the sun finds what's in the way.

Small objects cast their shadow: the taps over the schoolyard sink now shade the sink below them.
Bushes, trees and flower beds get depth: the leaves shade each other, so they are no longer flat green.
Under ledges and eaves: a thin dark line where a wall's cap, a roof edge or a planter sticks out.
Cheap: about 0.25 ms per frame at 4K in a sunny town, less in the shade.

They only come from what's on screen, so something just outside the picture casts none. Darkness under benches
and in corners is a different effect (ambient occlusion), not this one. In the panel (F1, SHADOWS, CONTACT
SHADOWS) to compare.
Off and on, same spot:

Anti-aliasing: FXAA, SMAA and TAA, with the UI kept sharp
The Switch version has none. Three kinds are in, all applied to the 3D scene before the UI is
drawn, so text and menus stay sharp:

FXAA: fast, smooths jagged edges in one frame.
SMAA: sharper edge smoothing than FXAA, also one frame at a time.
TAA: also fixes shimmer. Thin things (fences, the goal net, wires, leaves) fall between pixels differently
every frame, so they crawl while the camera moves. TAA shifts the 3D scene by a fraction of a pixel each frame and
blends the frames together, using the motion the game already writes for every pixel. In the schoolyard the goal
net breaks into dots and dashes without AA; with TAA it is a continuous mesh. A light sharpen keeps textures crisp
(decision 0032).

Yo-kai World with TAA, 21:9 at 4K height (5120×2160):

The same frame zoomed in 3×: the red railing, the fence by the lamp post and the road line.

Texture filtering: anisotropic up to ×16, sharp ground into the distance
The Switch version uses none, so the ground blurs a short way ahead of the camera. Anisotropic
filtering keeps the road, pavement and walls sharp into the distance, even at a low angle. Yo-kai World with ×16:

The same spot zoomed in 2×: the crosswalk far ahead, the pavement on the right and the road surface.

Performance

Frame rate: 30, 60, 120, 144 or no limit, switchable while playing
FRAME RATE in the settings panel: the game's 30 frames/s, or 60, 120, 144 or no limit. The game already moves by the real time between frames, so walking, battles, menus and cutscenes all work at any rate (~140 frames/s at 1600×900). At 4K the GPU is the limit: upscaling lifts it, frame generation doubles what is shown.

Upscaling (NVIDIA DLSS, AMD FSR): the world drawn smaller, rebuilt at full size, menus kept sharp
With ANTI-ALIASING set to DLSS or FSR, the UPSCALING row draws the 3D world smaller than the resolution and the
upscaler rebuilds a full-size picture from it and the frames before, using the motion the game writes. The menus
and text are drawn afterwards at full size.
Which to use: DLSS for the cleanest picture, FSR for the most frames. On an NVIDIA RTX GPU, DLSS keeps fine
patterns (perforated fences, leaves) clean where FSR turns them to grain, and shadow edges still. It uses NVIDIA's
newest model, which costs more GPU time than FSR; with it, balanced is the fastest DLSS mode (its performance
mode uses a heavier model). FSR runs on any GPU and gives more frames in every mode. DLSS needs NVIDIA RTX;
choosing it elsewhere falls back to FSR.

316zgc.title: Danganronpa 2×2 details Akimbo Consensus system, refined returning systems
316zgc.content:
PCPS5SwitchSwitch 2Xbox Series

Watch the new systems trailer.
Publisher Spike Chunsoft and developer Gemdrops have released new information, video, and screenshots for Danganronpa 2×2 introducing details about the Class Trials featured in Slayhem Mode, including the new Akimbo Consensus system. Here are the details:■ A New Class Trial System: Akimbo ConsensusWhen a murder occurs among the students, an initial investigation takes place, followed by a Class Trial. This is where Slayhem mode introduces the new Akimbo Consensus system.During a Class Trial, parties may voice various, often conflicting, testimonies, causing the discussion to become chaotic and difficult to follow. This is the point where Akimbo Consensus comes into play. You must evaluate the validity of each statement and use either an “Affirm” or “Refute” Truth Bullet to address it, thereby organizing the discussion and steering it in the right direction.
Once you have correctly organized the statements, three options will appear at the end, allowing you to decide what should be discussed next. If you make the appropriate choice, it is considered a “Consensus,” and the Akimbo Consensus is successful. The Class Trial will then proceed in the direction you have established.Slayhem Mode Also Utilizes a Familiar System From a Previous TitleSlayhem mode also includes the Debate Scrum that was featured in Danganronpa V3: Killing Harmony. A Debate Scrum is a team-based trial battle that happens during Class Trials when the students split into two opposing groups with conflicting opinions.■ Class Trials in Original Mode Have Also Been RefinedRebuttal ShowdownThis occurs when other students challenge the deductions made by the protagonist, Hajime Hinata. You can slice through their statements using Truth Blades, an element that offers a unique gameplay experience.Logic DiveIn Logic Dive, you’ll navigate a tube-like course representing a path of synapses in the brain, dodging obstacles and answering questions along the way. Known for its high difficulty in previous game, this version includes features designed to make the experience more accessible to players.Danganronpa 2×2 is due out for PlayStation 5, Xbox Series, Switch 2, Switch, and PC via Steam and Epic Games Store on January 14, 2027.Watch the trailer below. h70kqf.title: Could your personality be affecting how you feel about social media?
h70kqf.byline: Claire Hart, Carmen Șurariu, Kathy Carnelley
h70kqf.content:
Credit: JÉSHOOTS from Pexels

Social media offers everyone the same basic promise: post something about yourself and get responses from other people. Whether it's a vacation, a promotion or just a midweek meal, these days many people's lives are shared online.

But could it be that what users feel they get back from the exchange depends on their personality? Our research published in Behaviour & Information Technology has found that people who are higher in a trait called "narcissistic admiration" tend to be more positive about their online interactions. Narcissistic admiration is when someone goes out of their way to attract attention and validation as a way of boosting their self-esteem.
At the same time, those higher in narcissistic rivalry (positioning themselves as superior to others) and narcissistic vulnerability (those struggling with insecurity) reported fewer favorable social outcomes.
We initially thought differences in how they presented themselves online might help to explain these differences. But when we followed people's actual social media posts over three weeks, we found that wasn't the case. Instead, our findings pointed toward another possibility. What people expect from social media, and whether they feel they get it, may be an important part of the story.
We often use the term "narcissistic" to describe someone who loves attention. But narcissistic traits exist on a continuum—we all have them to some degree. Psychologists also distinguish between narcissistic traits.
Narcissistic admiration involves wanting to stand out, impress others and gain admiration and status. Narcissistic rivalry is more antagonistic and involves maintaining superiority, partly by devaluing others.
Vulnerable narcissism looks different. People higher in this trait tend to have a more fragile sense of self and greater sensitivity to rejection and how they feel they are being judged by their peers.

What people really think of us
Social media is an interesting environment in which to study these traits. It offers opportunities to attract attention and admiration, but also frequent feedback about whether other people have responded as we hoped.
In our research, we examined more than 1,000 social media users across Brazil, Indonesia and the U.K. Participants completed questionnaires measuring their levels of narcissistic admiration, rivalry and vulnerability, alongside questions about what they felt they gained from their social media interactions.
People higher in narcissistic admiration tended to feel they gained more from their social media interactions. This included factors such as greater levels of attention and validation, and more opportunities to initiate relationships.
Those higher in narcissistic rivalry and vulnerability reported less favorable experiences. They felt less close to others and that they received less attention. This raised an obvious question: Why?
One possibility was that people with different narcissistic traits were simply presenting themselves differently online. So, in another paper published in the Journal of Research in Personality, we looked much more closely at what happened in people's everyday social media lives.
We followed 154 adults over 21 days, repeatedly asking them about posts they had made. Participants told us what they expected to get from their posts and, later, what they felt they had received. We also asked about their well-being.

Some of the patterns we'd found previously appeared again. People higher in narcissistic admiration reported more favorable daily interpersonal outcomes. Those higher in rivalry reported poorer outcomes when it came to relationships—that is, initiating them, maintaining them and staying close to people. Vulnerable narcissism was associated with lower levels of closeness and less ability to maintain relationships.
But differences in how people presented themselves online didn't explain this variation in perceived social outcomes. Instead, people's expectations provided an intriguing clue.
People higher in vulnerable narcissism expected to be more popular and get more attention and validation from their social media posts than they subsequently felt they received.
Vulnerable narcissism was also consistently associated with lower well-being in this study. And when people expected a post to help manage their relationships but then felt that it hadn't, this mismatch was more keenly felt among those with higher levels of vulnerable narcissism.
This doesn't mean that unmet expectations caused poorer well-being. Nor did we objectively count every like, comment or message that our participants received. Our findings concern people's perceptions of what they got back.
But it suggests that understanding people's experiences of social media may require looking beyond what they post. Who we are and what we expect from other people may matter too.

So what can we do with this? Our findings don't suggest that people should simply expect less from social media. Wanting connection, attention or reassurance from other people is a normal part of life.
But they do suggest that it may be useful to think about what we are expecting a post to achieve. Are we sharing something because we want to connect with others? Are we looking for reassurance or validation? Are we hoping that one particular person will respond?
If the response feels disappointing, it may be worth considering not only what came back, but also what we had hoped would happen. Becoming more aware of those expectations may help us to understand our own reactions to social media. Otherwise, we could assume that how we feel is simply a consequence of the response itself.
There is a broader lesson here too. Discussions about whether social media is "good" or "bad" for our well-being often focus on platforms, screen time or what people post. Our findings add another layer: the same online environment may be experienced very differently depending on the person using it and what they hope to get from it.

More information
Carmen Șurariu et al., Me, myself, and my profile: social media self-presentation and perceived social benefits across cultural contexts, as shaped by narcissism, Behaviour & Information Technology (2026). DOI: 10.1080/0144929x.2026.2732026
Carmen Șurariu et al., Day by day on display: A daily diary study of narcissists' social media self-presentation, perceptions of social outcomes, and subjective well-being, Journal of Research in Personality (2026). DOI: 10.1016/j.jrp.2026.104727

Who's behind this story?

Robert Egan

Bachelor's in mathematical biology, Master's in creative writing. Well-traveled with unique perspectives on science and language.

The intention behind this change is to alleviate that striking difference. By narrowing the area affected by the explosion we have made it so that players cannot reap the maximum benefit without using it at the precise position. 1dnr7q3.title: Baby, she's back: SpaceX catches a Starship from orbit for first time
1dnr7q3.content:
The Starship rocket's second stage, known as Ship 42, hangs from a set of giant mechanical arms on the launch tower at SpaceX's Starbase launch pad in Texas. Credit: SpaceX via X

SpaceX brought back its Starship rocket's second stage today for a first-ever midair capture at its launch pad, capping a record-setting orbital flight test.

The 171-foot-tall (52-meter) space vehicle, known as Ship 42, settled between a giant pair of mechanical arms extended from the South Texas launch tower where its journey began 22.5 hours earlier. The arm-capture system, nicknamed "Mechazilla," had been used three times previously to capture Starship Super Heavy boosters during suborbital flight tests, but this was the first time for a second stage coming in hot from orbit.
"Mechazilla has caught the Starship—we've been waiting to hear that for a long time," SpaceX launch commentator Dan Huot said.
In addition to the first orbital catch, this week's test marked the longest Starship flight to date, besting a three-hour orbital flight in September.
Years of development—including 15 full-scale flight tests since 2023—led up to today's orbital catch, which Huot called "the Holy Grail of spaceflight." The achievement took the sting out of the previous day's aborted effort to catch the rocket's booster using the same system, minutes after liftoff. SpaceX said the booster was diverted when its onboard system detected a fuel-system alarm. The root cause of the alarm is under investigation.

Starship first catch. Credit: SciNews
SpaceX plans to use the launch-pad arms to recover Starship's boosters and second stages on a routine basis, achieving company founder Elon Musk's goal of creating a fully reusable, orbital-class launch system.
This 15th flight test proceeded almost in textbook fashion, aside from the booster's offshore splashdown on launch day. During the first hours of its 14-orbit flight, Starship deployed 26 more next-generation satellites for SpaceX's Starlink broadband internet network. All of the satellites were in good health and beginning to raise their orbits to operational altitude, the company said.

At the end of the trip, the second stage fired a single engine for roughly 10 seconds to start its descent through the atmosphere. As the temperatures rose, a bright glow surrounded Ship 42's leading edges. The craft executed a bellyflop maneuver to maximize its deceleration. Then it righted itself and fired its engines a final time to sink into Mechazilla's arms.
SpaceX employees around the country and hundreds of onlookers near the Texas launch site cheered, while "Baby, Come Back" played on the soundtrack for the webcast. "Baby, she's back," Huot joked.
Bringing Starship into full operation is expected to speed up deployment of Starlink satellites. More importantly, Starship is slated to serve as a landing system for NASA's crewed moon missions starting as early as 2028. Starship and Blue Origin's Blue Moon landing system are scheduled for testing in low Earth orbit next year during NASA's Artemis III mission.
In a post to X, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman congratulated Musk and the SpaceX team on today's successful catch. "It was almost magic ... Making more believers by the day," he wrote. Using emojis, Isaacman said the achievement brought the United States "one step closer" to putting an American flag once more on the moon.

SpaceX's team will analyze the data gathered about Starship's performance, including the ability of Ship 42's heat shield to stand up to the rigors of atmospheric reentry. The company is gearing up to expand Starship operations to NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida, and yet another Starship launch site is in the works for Louisiana.
In the long term, Musk envisions creating a fleet of Starships that could offer point-to-point rocket travel on Earth, as well as mass transit to Mars and other off-Earth destinations. Cryptocurrency investor Chun Wang has already announced his intention to take Starship trips around the moon and Mars.
"I don't think you guys understand," a software engineer named Will DePue wrote in a post to X. "You will get the chance to go to space in your lifetime. New era."
"Yes," Musk replied.

816rcs.title: Flat optics roadmap charts path toward smaller imaging and sensing systems
816rcs.content:
Representative examples of space–time metasurfaces for nonreciprocal propagation, dynamic wavefront control, and frequency conversion. Credit: Journal of Nanophotonics (2026). DOI: 10.1117/1.jnp.20.030901

For centuries, optical systems have relied on lenses, mirrors and other components that manipulate light through their shape and size. Today, advances in nanotechnology are enabling a different approach. Researchers can now engineer materials at scales smaller than the wavelength of light, creating ultrathin optical components that offer new ways to control how light behaves.

A new roadmap published in the Journal of Nanophotonics examines the rapid evolution of optical meta-devices and outlines the developments that could shape the field in the coming years. This roadmap, led by a team at City University of Hong Kong and RIKEN Center for Advanced Photonics, surveys progress in metamaterials and metasurfaces, technologies that are helping transform optical systems from assemblies of bulky components into compact, multifunctional devices.
Flat optics shrink imaging systems
Metasurfaces consist of carefully designed arrays of nanoscale structures that can manipulate the phase, amplitude and polarization of light. Because these capabilities can be incorporated into ultrathin, planar optical elements, metasurfaces offer an alternative to many traditional optical components. This shift toward flat optics could enable smaller and lighter imaging, sensing and communication systems.
Among the most active areas of research are metalenses, flat optical devices that focus light without the curved glass used in conventional lenses. The roadmap highlights recent advances in metalens performance and their integration into compact imaging systems, reflecting ongoing efforts to simplify conventional optical assemblies and develop more compact optical systems.

Progress in physical principles and control, computational design, device functionalities and system integration will help translate flat-optics research into practical technologies for imaging, sensing, communications and optical computing. Credit: Rong Lin et al.

Smarter designs and tunable devices
The roadmap also points to artificial intelligence and inverse-design techniques as increasingly important tools for developing future metadevices. Designing nanoscale optical structures involves navigating an enormous number of possible geometries. Data-driven approaches are helping researchers identify designs that would be difficult to discover through conventional methods alone, while improving performance and reducing development time.
Another major area of progress charted by the roadmap involves reconfigurable metasurfaces. By combining metasurfaces with tunable materials and microelectromechanical systems, researchers are creating devices whose optical properties can be adjusted after fabrication. Such systems could support adaptive imaging and sensing technologies capable of responding to changing conditions in real time.
The roadmap further explores advances in nonlinear optics, ultrasensitive sensing, holography, augmented and virtual reality displays, and quantum imaging. Increasingly, metasurfaces are being integrated with detectors, emitters and other active components, bringing the technology closer to practical optical systems rather than standalone laboratory demonstrations.

Scaling production for practical optical systems
Corresponding author Din Ping Tsai notes, "While significant technical challenges remain, particularly in large-scale manufacturing and system integration, the field is witnessing steady progress toward fabrication methods compatible with established semiconductor processes." The roadmap identifies scalable production and integration as key steps for translating research advances into commercial optical technologies.
By bringing together developments across multiple areas of research, the roadmap presents a snapshot of a field moving from fundamental discovery toward real-world implementation. As advances in materials, design and manufacturing continue to converge, optical meta-devices are expected to play an increasingly important role in next-generation imaging, sensing, communications and quantum technologies.

More information
Rong Lin et al., Roadmap for optical meta-devices based on metamaterials, Journal of Nanophotonics (2026). DOI: 10.1117/1.jnp.20.030901

121wg4v.title: Early black holes may have grown through productive chaos
121wg4v.content:
Relation between the average growth timescale and required seed mass for selected SMBHs with z > 7.5, assuming seed formation at t = 100 Myr (z = 30). Credit: Astronomy & Astrophysics (2026). DOI: 10.1051/0004-6361/202558523

When the universe was less than 700 million years old, the supermassive black hole powering a quasar called J0313-1806 had already grown to about 3 billion times the mass of the sun. It is one of the most extreme examples of a puzzle that has occupied astrophysicists for two decades: How did supermassive black holes grow so big so quickly?

At its core, the puzzle is a speed limit. A black hole grows by swallowing, or accreting, gas, but the infalling matter heats up and shines, and the radiation pushes on the gas still arriving. At the so-called Eddington limit, radiation pressure balances gravity and infall cannot speed up further. Because this limit scales with the black hole's mass, growth is exponential. If, as usually assumed, about 10% of the infalling mass is converted to radiation, the mass grows by a factor of e (about 2.7) every 45 million years.
A stellar-mass black hole of about a hundred solar masses would need about 17 such steps, roughly 770 million years, to reach 3 billion solar masses. When you account for the time it took for the stellar black holes to form, the universe had less than 600 million years available.
There are two popular ways out. One is to start with a "heavy seed" of at least 10,000 solar masses, formed by the direct collapse of enormous gas clouds. This would skip the slowest part of the climb. The other is to break the Eddington limit: If the energy released by infalling gas is removed in ways other than radiation, the black hole can grow far faster. Both options have caveats: Direct collapse requires a rare combination of conditions, and it is uncertain whether real accretion flows can stay super-Eddington for hundreds of millions of years.
In a new paper with my colleague Matas Tartėnas, published in Astronomy & Astrophysics, we ask whether a third, older and simpler idea survives confrontation with the latest data. It is called chaotic accretion, and it needs neither a heavy seed nor a broken speed limit.

Why a spinning-down black hole grows faster
The "chaos" in our model comes from how gas reaches the black hole. We consider a slowly rotating dark matter halo, so that gas falls in from essentially random directions. Each stream forms a small disk, tilted randomly relative to the black hole's spin, feeds it briefly and is quickly followed by another, tilted differently. Some episodes spin the black hole up; others, where the disk counter-rotates, spin it down. Spin-down is rarer but more efficient per unit of mass, so over time the spin stays low.
That matters because a slowly spinning black hole converts less of the infalling mass into light: It radiates away only about 6 to 7.5% of the mass it swallows, rather than 10%. This may seem like a small difference, but it shortens the growth timescale from 45 to roughly 27–32 million years, and the time required to grow J0313-1806 from 770 to 550 million years.
In this scenario, the gas supply on large scales can exceed the rate necessary for the Eddington limit. What matters, though, is how much material reaches the event horizon, and that stays near the Eddington rate, while most of the rest is removed along the way. The large gas reservoir, however, ensures that the black hole may be fed nearly continuously.
What the data say
We compared this prediction with mass estimates for all known supermassive black holes at redshifts above seven. The most reliable (virial) estimates, out to redshift 10.6 and including J0313-1806, can all be explained by a seed of about 100 solar masses or smaller, formed around 100 million years after the Big Bang, growing on a timescale of about 32 million years. This requires almost continuous feeding at least 85% of the time at the Eddington rate, or all the time at 85% of it.
This shows that the scenario works, not that the alternatives fail. Our scenario cannot explain several existing mass estimates, but those are made using methods that rely on more assumptions about the accretion flow. For example, for the galaxy GN-z11, the virial estimate is about seven times lower than the less robust one. Several more distant black holes lack robust masses and would make excellent near-future observation targets.

How to tell the scenarios apart
We also propose ways to distinguish the three explanations. Chaotic accretion predicts slow spins for the most massive early black holes, while sustained super-Eddington growth should leave them spinning rapidly. Spin can be measured from the shape of X-ray emission lines, but current measurements are at lower redshifts and ambiguous. ESA's planned NewAthena observatory is best suited to the task, but it won't launch until at least 2037.
In our scenario, the maximum black hole mass should rise very rapidly until redshift 7.5 and then nearly plateau. Current data hint at this but cover too little volume to be conclusive; wide-area surveys such as Euclid and Roman should find enough black holes to test it. In particular, a robustly measured black hole of more than a billion solar masses at redshift 9.1 or higher would falsify our model.
Finally, once a rapidly growing black hole reaches 100,000 to 10 million solar masses, depending on its halo, its accretion energy can drive large-scale outflows that clear the surrounding gas and make it visible, possibly as a "little red dot," a compact and bright source of the kind discovered by the James Webb Space Telescope. The inferred little red dot masses fall in this range, although what powers them is still debated.
For now, our conclusion is modest. Ordinary stellar-mass seeds growing near the Eddington limit with low spin can explain the earliest known supermassive black holes, without invoking massive seeds or super-Eddington growth. Whether that is what actually happened is a question the next generation of telescopes can answer.
This story is part of Science X Dialog, where researchers can report findings from their published research articles. Visit this page for information about Science X Dialog and how to participate.

Publication details
K. Zubovas et al., Chaotic accretion can (still) explain early supermassive black hole growth, Astronomy & Astrophysics (2026). DOI: 10.1051/0004-6361/202558523

1mol79h.title: 'Buffer spaces' may help resolve workplace concerns
1mol79h.content:
Reporting Process Drawn by HR. Credit: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction (2026). DOI: 10.1145/3816937

Nearly every person will run into conflict in their workplace at some point in their career, but it can be difficult to know when or how to report these concerns.

A study by researchers at the University of California, Santa Cruz, explores how workers use technology to report workplace concerns and finds there is a lot of gray space between informal conversations and formal reporting. In a paper published in the Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction, the scholars introduce the concept of buffer spaces, which sit between informal and formal workplace conflict resolution and can offer a path toward resolution.
The study won a best paper award at the 2026 ACM Conference on Computer-Supported Cooperative Work and Social Computing.
"When workplace concerns don't get reported, they don't just disappear," said Peiyao Liu, a doctoral student in computational media and the study's lead author. "They build up, and people get burned out. Understanding how people actually decide whether to speak up matters for everyone, not just the person with the problem."
Digging into issues with concern reporting
Liu carried out this research with associate professor of computational media Norman Su, who leads the Authentic User Experience Lab at the Baskin School of Engineering, and associate professor Lynn Dombrowski at Georgia Tech's School of Interactive Computing. Su's group studies the relationship of technology with subcultures, using methods like interviews and surveys to better understand people's pain points with technology in everyday life and offer design guidelines.

"We want to offer some direction for future researchers to think about why current channels or technology don't work, and how we can design the tools to support them," Liu said.
Su and Liu are interested in workplace concern reporting because it's a widespread and often painful issue, but one that can be particularly challenging for people with marginalized identities.
"The people who stay quiet are always the ones who need help the most—women in male-dominated teams, LGBTQ employees, people of color or people with disabilities," Liu said. "For them, speaking up can feel riskier."
The researchers, who are based at the UC Santa Cruz Silicon Valley Campus, set out to better understand how employees and HR professionals use formal systems, backchannel conversations and everything in between to resolve issues. They partnered with the Bay Area Human Resources Executives Council, which holds meetings at the Silicon Valley Campus, to learn and get feedback on their work.
Past research on workplace reporting tends to focus on the two far ends of the reporting spectrum: staying silent and filing formal complaints. But in interviews with 22 participants, including 10 employees from various industries and 12 HR professionals, the researchers found people's real experiences tend to fall somewhere in between.
People may turn to conversations in person, on messaging platforms like Slack or on social media for comfort, validation and support, but this may not always lead to real solutions. Meanwhile, formal reporting resources can be seen as untrustworthy, difficult to use and ultimately ineffective, and workers may fear retribution.

Buffer spaces can offer a path forward
This space in between informal conversations and formal reporting is what the researchers call buffer spaces. What they look like might vary in different workplaces, but they might be a dedicated Slack workspace, technology administered by an employee resource group (ERG) or even a specially trained chatbot.
Whatever the format, in order to be effective, the researchers say buffer spaces should provide a setting for workers to slow down and deliberate, and have low-pressure entry points. They should also provide a pathway for workers to move their complaints toward individual or collective action, if needed. Making these decisions earlier can help prevent problems from spiraling into an issue that is impossible to resolve.
"The question is, how might we support the transition period from informal talk to action?" Su said. "Buffer spaces could give people that door to say, 'I think it's not a big deal, or I can deal with it by talking with people,' or, 'I should move it to a formal action and report something.'"
Additionally, buffer spaces must be built on a foundation of trust and privacy, Liu said, to effectively resolve issues. This would influence how technology like surveys or AI systems are developed and used—an area of future research for the scholars.
"I think there are a lot of really interesting challenges in how you would implement buffer space and have technologies help along that process," Su said. "There are huge privacy implications and trust ones, but I think that's what makes it an interesting research problem."
These buffer spaces can also support HR professionals, who often must walk a tricky line between supporting employees and representing their employer. Buffer spaces can offer the opportunity to build trust and hear complaints earlier, when there might be more potential for a successful resolution.

More information
Peiyao Liu et al., From Mediation to Escalation: Buffer Spaces for Workplace Concern Reporting, Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction (2026). DOI: 10.1145/3816937

6ul1vt.title: Sensor Tower: GTA 6 pre-orders exceed $1.4bn, with 87% for the Ultimate Edition
6ul1vt.content:
Pre-orders rose sixfold on the day Netflix premiered the Extended Look of the game, reaching $16.3 million

Image credit: Rockstar Games

Sensor Tower estimates Grand Theft Auto 6 has generated over $1.4 billion in pre-order revenue, with 87% of orders for the Ultimate Edition.
As detailed in a new report on the game's impact on consumer engagement, pre-orders rose sixfold when Netflix released its Extended Look at the game on August 27.
According to Sensor Tower, daily GTA 6 pre-order revenue across PlayStation and Xbox ranged from $2.4 million to $3.8 million through "most of" August.
Revenue reached $16.3 million the day after the Netflix special and has continued to rise ahead of launch, making GTA 6 the most pre-ordered game on PlayStation and Xbox storefronts.
The market intelligence firm also analysed which games are most likely to lose players to GTA 6. Fortnite, GTA Online, and other AAA single-player titles are expected to be most affected.
Among PlayStation users, 42% with GTA 5 also own Fortnite, compared to 22% of all players. Sensor Tower noted that "Fortnite and Roblox seem [the] most exposed from an audience overlap perspective."
Sensor Tower expects Roblox to retain its player base during GTA 6's launch. It noted Roblox "beat the catalogue in player count change in the month following five recent releases," including Monster Hunter Wilds, Oblivion Remastered, Resident Evil Requiem, Crimson Desert, and First Light.
"Roblox's audience looks less likely to be lured away by acclaimed single-player launches, and is likely to weather GTA 6 better than its peers," the firm suggested.
Last month, gaming consultancy Open World assessed which games might lose players to GTA 6. Fortnite, Call of Duty, Battlefield, Apex Legends, EA Sports FC, and NBA 2K were identified as most at risk during GTA 6's launch.

1mlr3yr.title: AI could help speed up research ethics approvals
1mlr3yr.content:
Comparison of processing times across different large language models (LLMs). Credit: Scientific Reports (2026). DOI: 10.1038/s41598-026-62027-y

Artificial intelligence programs could be used to improve efficiency for professionals dealing with research ethics reviews, enabling humans to focus on the ethical decision-making.

New University of Bristol research published in Scientific Reports on Nov. 16 has found large language models were able to check research applications against published standards within minutes—however, performance varied significantly between models.
Claude leads on accuracy and speed
The study, conducted in collaboration with the Health Research Authority (HRA), tested three widely used large language models (Claude 3.5 Sonnet, ChatGPT-4o and Microsoft Copilot) on a task that currently requires substantial human time: checking research ethics applications against the HRA's published quality standards.
The results showed significant differences between the tools. Claude achieved fully correct answers to 87.9% of checks, compared with 66.5% for ChatGPT and 62.8% for Copilot. It was also the fastest, taking an average of just over seven minutes to assess each application.
The findings suggest AI could help reduce the administrative burden associated with research approvals, allowing staff to devote more time to the ethical questions that require human judgment.
Lead author Dr. Panos Maghsoudlou, NIHR academic clinical lecturer in ophthalmology in the School of Biochemistry and Biomedical Sciences, said: "These results highlight both the potential of AI-assisted checking and the risks of relying on its outputs without verification.
"Large language models could be used to support the early stages of the research approval process, identifying missing information and potential departures from published standards before applications reach an ethics committee. By automating routine checks, AI could help reduce administrative workloads and enable approvals staff and committee members to concentrate on the substantive ethical issues at the heart of research review."

Testing the limits of automated checks
Before a research study can begin, its application must undergo checks which can involve reviewing hundreds of pages and comparing information across multiple documents.
Although essential, these types of tasks can be time-consuming and account for a significant proportion of the approval process. The new study examined whether large language models could undertake these checks, comparing their accuracy, speed and response quality, as well as the types of errors they made.
All three models were able to carry out checks against the HRA's quality standards, but their performance varied considerably.
Claude answered every question and completed each application in an average of seven minutes. ChatGPT took an average of 13 minutes, while Copilot took 23 minutes. Copilot also failed to answer data protection questions in most applications.
The differences were particularly striking when the models were assessed on their ability to identify problems requiring correction. Claude identified an average of eight errors per application, compared with 2.3 for ChatGPT and 1.3 for Copilot.
There were also differences in how well the LLMs performed. Failures in logical reasoning were the most common source of inaccurate responses across all three models. Claude produced fewer hallucinations—instances in which an AI system generates information that is incorrect or unsupported—than the other tools.

Human judgment remains central
Maghsoudlou added, "The findings also underline an important distinction: checking whether an application meets documented requirements is not the same as deciding whether a study is ethically acceptable. The latter requires human judgment and cannot be reduced to a checklist.
"The research therefore points toward a potential role for AI as an assistant to the approval process, rather than a replacement for researchers, approvals staff or ethics committees."
Dr. Jonathan Fennelly-Barnwell, director of approvals at the HRA, and the co-author of the paper, said, "We collaborated on this study to explore and develop an evidence base on how AI could potentially be used to support the streamlining of research approval processes.
"The study demonstrated how AI could be used for specific routine checks before a study is reviewed by a research ethics committee or HRA staff. The benefit of using AI in this way is that it could release staff capacity to focus on more complex regulatory issues, making our processes more effective and potentially also helping reduce the timeline for regulatory review.
"While the results of the study are promising, further exploration will be required before we can make recommendations for how we might be able to adopt AI to improve our processes. This is why we are continuing to test and evaluate the safe and responsible use of AI as part of our wider work to explore its benefits and challenges."

Publication details
Panagiotis Maghsoudlou et al., Evaluating large language models for quality control in research ethics review, Scientific Reports (2026). DOI: 10.1038/s41598-026-62027-y

1y0hs3x.title: Flip side: Upside-down atomic layers could steer heat in stacked computer chips
1y0hs3x.content:
Visual Abstract. Credit: ACS Nano (2026). DOI: 10.1021/acsnano.6c07922

Stacking chips on top of one another could keep computers getting faster, but it creates a heating problem. Now, researchers from Japan have found that simply flipping atom-thin layers upside down could help steer that heat where it needs to go.

In a study recently published in ACS Nano, researchers from the Institute of Industrial Science, The University of Tokyo, and their collaborators propose "flipping engineering," a new way to design layered materials that readily conduct heat along their layers while strongly blocking heat flow between them.
In three-dimensional integrated circuits, semiconductor chips are stacked vertically. This can cause heat to build up between the layers and travel from high-power computing chips into neighboring components such as memory. To prevent this, engineers need materials that act like a radiator in one direction and an insulating blanket in the other.
Searching thousands of flipping sequences
"Our approach uses Janus atomic layers, whose two faces consist of different atomic species," says lead author of the study Xin Wu. "Because the top and bottom are different, we can choose the orientation of each stacked layer individually, right side up or upside down, almost like a game of Tetris. This gives us a simple, programmable switch for designing the structure."
The team focused on MoSSe, a molybdenum-based material with sulfur atoms on one face and selenium atoms on the other. A 14-layer stack can be arranged in 8,192 different flipping sequences, far too many to test individually. Instead, the researchers built a machine-learning workflow combining thermal transport prediction with stacking optimization to find the best candidate.

Heat flow favors one direction
After evaluating only about 3% of the possible configurations, they identified a structure whose in-plane thermal conductivity is approximately 760 times its effective cross-plane thermal conductivity at room temperature. This thermal anisotropy ratio is about 35% higher than that of an ordered crystalline stack of the same thickness.
"The irregular flipping sequence disrupts the vibrations that carry heat between the layers," explains senior author Masahiro Nomura. "Importantly, it leaves the vibrations that carry heat along the layers essentially untouched, so we can selectively suppress cross-plane heat transport while largely preserving in-plane thermal conductivity."
Although fabrication and experimental validation remain challenges for the future, existing layer-by-layer assembly techniques, including methods that can flip individual layers, offer a possible route to building such structures. The findings provide a new material design principle that could help improve thermal management in three-dimensional semiconductor chips.

Publication details
Xin Wu et al., Data-Driven Flipping Engineering for High Thermal Anisotropy in Janus Two-Dimensional Materials, ACS Nano (2026). DOI: 10.1021/acsnano.6c07922
