1obl199.title: Parker Posey Knows Career Highs and Lows. Right Now, She’s Having a Blast
1obl199.content:
“I’ve never done anything like this,” Parker Posey says. She has certainly, over her singular 35-year screen career, sat down with journalists plenty, and likely on this very couch at the Chateau Marmont, where she’s been staying over a busy weekend of events in Los Angeles. But our meeting has come on the heels of a dizzying press run for Posey, one that feels as much about her entire life onscreen as it is about her fresh projects that are ripe for promotion — most significantly, her small but vivid role in Martin McDonagh’s new Oscar-bound film, Wild Horse Nine.

“I don’t really have a reference point to this because I just got a publicist a few years ago,” Posey says, between sips of her grapefruit juice. While the sustained exposure — the periods of talking about oneself, really — could seem daunting, you sense quickly that Posey approaches it like she does anything else. She excitedly orders olives and almonds and crudité for our lounge table. She happily ignores our time limit, even if she’ll have to hail an Uber across town to meet some friends for lunch. She makes strong, direct eye contact, constantly shifting between my questions and her own curiosity about the person sitting before her. “I bet we have friends in common,” she says at one point.

There’s nobody like Parker Posey, and this has been true for a long time across movies and TV. It’s why she remains so synonymous with the great American indie-film run of the ‘90s, why she can now both go viral with a single scream of a line — see recent HBO examples in The Staircase and, of course, The White Lotus — and still imbue the dialogue with surprising, heartfelt depth. And it’s perhaps why, as Posey finally, really puts herself out there, there’s a lot of love coming her way. You’ll see it in the thrill of her pulling out a title at random in the Criterion Closet, selecting Ghost World, and cheering, “I love this movie — yay!” Or in the warmth of her reviving her old bond with CBS Sunday Mornings correspondent Mo Rocca, as they quote Katharine Hepburn back and forth, grinning ear to ear.

“You’re 15 again, at North Carolina School of the Arts with your gay bestie — well, we didn’t say that [term] then,” Posey says of being interviewed by Rocca for that plum segment. “It was so meaningful to me. Because you’re always going to feel the same — you’ll just keep getting older. And it’s true, I do still feel the same. I feel like that person, excited to be at NCSA with Maurice.”

Parker Posey in Wild Horse Nine.

Justin Lubin/Searchlight Pictures

We’re speaking on a Monday afternoon, with Parker fresh off of her first ever Governors Awards — another point to reinforce that she truly is new to a lot of this. “I wanted to meet Paul Giamatti, and I saw Emma Stone — we did Irrational Man together, and I loved seeing her — so she brought me to him,” Posey says. “Then I met him and I was like, ‘I waved to you once in Citarella. I was like, Hey, and you waved back.’ It was just so silly. I’m just a fan.”

In Wild Horse Nine, Posey portrays Marge Chesterfield, wife of Lee (Sam Rockwell), a CIA agent on assignment in Chile ahead of the 1973 coup d’état. When Lee’s longtime mentor Chris (John Malkovich) drags him to Easter Island under mysterious circumstances, they wind up in the CIA’s crosshairs — which then puts Marge in peril back home in the US. Posey’s scenes play out over the phone opposite Rockwell, as Marge wrestles with the distance, the resentment and the sudden bizarre stakes of her marriage.

Posey and Rockwell traveled to each other to enhance their scenes as much as possible. “I still got to go to Easter Island and was there for Sam — there was so much that was allowed for, to have the actors feel connected to the story,” Posey says. She and Rockwell have known each other for decades, their first screen credit dating back to 1996’s Basquiat: “We’re brother and sister. We came up the same way.” This comes through even over the wired landline — it’s only the latest example of Posey finding her way into a smaller role before leaving an indelible mark. “I did lots of traveling. I had to chase down my jumpsuit and chase down Christian Siriano,” she says. “It was really charming. You can see the love there and the chemistry there.”

**

Posey first heard about Wild Horse Nine while she was in Bangkok, shooting the third season of The White Lotus — the first project, arguably, to hail this new Posey Appreciation era and bring her into the public eye in a larger way. She ran into Rockwell, who was also in the cast by creator Mike White in a smaller part, and asked what he’d be getting up to next. He told her he was reuniting with McDonagh for his next movie.

“I was like, ‘Are there any women in this?’” Posey recalls. “Of course, the writers [in Hollywood] are mostly male — that’s the place that they’re working from. I mean, and it’s a man’s world.” Fortunately, in Wild Horse Nine’s case, there were women — Posey’s feisty Marge feels of a piece with the great work done by Kerry Condon in The Banshees of Inisherin and Frances McDormand in Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri — but this is not the first time she’s asked that question when hearing about a compelling project. It says a lot about how she’s navigated life as a working actor.

Posey in The White Lotus.

Fabio Lovino/HBO

“Not only are stories so male-centric, but they forget about men and women together. We used to have that kind of play,” Posey says. This recalls her and Rocca’s recent, joyous quoting of Hepburn in On Golden Pond: “You’re my knight in shining armor. Don’t you forget it!”

Posey says now, “I still think they could do those movies now, those old movies that we loved that are on TCM — verbatim. The studios, since they own them — why aren’t they remaking them?”

Posey reflected on her own career while watching Glenn Close accept her honorary Oscar for lifetime achievement at the Governors Awards. “I love that turn that she made in Fatal Attraction — I don’t think I’d have the guts — but she had the support of the system, which I didn’t have,” Posey explains. “All these [indie] movies, I carried them for no money. Then I was asked to prove myself, which made me feel crazy.” She said “no” more often than others in her position might have; she didn’t play by typical Hollywood rules in the transition from the low-budget gems of Party Girl and Daytrippers to mainstream fare.

It’s not like Posey disappeared in the aughts and on — in reality, she found fascinating new shades, from stealing scenes in sitcoms like Will & Grace to continuing her brilliant work in Christopher Guest’s company. But to secure good work, and to make a living, it’s been a consistent fight. “My family and my friends had seen me struggle for a good 20 years,” Posey says. Then she corrects herself: “Maybe I’d say it’s always a struggle.”

As our food arrives, we discuss her innovative 2018 memoir You’re on an Airplane. “That was an interesting thing I had to do, writing my book,” she muses. I ask about that language — why did she have to do it? “I ran out of money,” she says flatly. “I had to sell my apartment.” She walks that phrasing back a tad — “Well, I didn’t run out” — but reiterates that the point stands: She was not in a good financial situation. Writing a memoir was necessary.

This, despite her never disappearing from our screens. “You go, ‘Oh, well, I’ll be right for something. I’ve always been right for something. Something will come up,’” Posey says. “And you get older and things aren’t coming up — because you’re older and you’re a woman. Then it’s kind of like, ‘I like this. Doesn’t pay me anything. But I love it.’ Do work for the sake of the work.”

One notable actor and former colleague once told Posey that she had “sabotaged” herself, career-wise; she recently discussed this incident with Rocca. “I was like, ‘I don’t know — if I did, then that was just proof that I wasn’t ready,’” Posey says to me now. I suggest that sabotage is an especially strong word. “Right: ‘Is that how you see it? Is that how you see my choices?’” she says. “Maybe I’m in the long game…. Every obstacle pushes you somewhere else as an artist, to where you have to be. It’s all a mix.”

Posey in The Staircase.

Around the time that Posey’s father passed away, she was offered a key role in HBO Max’s The Staircase, a sprawling true-crime drama toplined by awards magnets Colin Firth and Toni Collette, the latter of whom costarred with Posey 30 years ago in the indie cult favorite Clockwatchers. (Also starring in that movie, Lisa Kudrow: “I just saw Lisa a few weeks ago. She’s so wonderful. I love The Comeback so much. I love the surveillance cameras in the bedroom.”)

Posey instilled The Staircase’s role of prosecutor Freda Black with as much wild humor (ask her to deliver the line “fuck, suck and rim,” and she will deliver) as she did idiosyncratic realism. “My dad died and then I got asked to play a Southern woman on The Staircase and pay tribute to his side of the family,” she says. It’s one of her more underrated, deft performances, and it kicked off a hell of a streak. She jumped straight from there to Ari Aster’s Beau Is Afraid, where she shot one of the decade’s most memorably graphic death scenes. The next year made room for Posey’s guest spot in Mr. & Mrs. Smith, which resulted in her first Emmy nomination; the year after that was The White Lotus, netting her nomination no. 2 and so very many memes. Her hilarious, mesmerizing turn in Mike White’s dramedy, as the eminently quotable Victoria Ratliff, still pops up on social-media feeds on the daily. It brought Posey new fame, and cemented this new era of her career.

“My friends and family were relieved,” she says. “They were so happy. And then I started hearing from other people: ‘You deserve this, and you’ve worked really hard.’”

She sits on that line a bit as she grabs her last olive of the afternoon. “But it’s not work for me — it’s not, because I’m an artist,” she says. “I’m not working for a vacation. And isn’t that the life that I wanted?”

b8nyj9.title: When the Work Gets Heavy, Do Your Tires Hold Up? Cooper’s New Discoverer® HT Is Built to Carry the Weight
b8nyj9.content: For enthusiasts, tire shopping is an upgrade, not a chore. While the casual driver might treat new tires like regular maintenance, anyone who cares about vehicle dynamics knows that what meets the road defines how a truck or SUV rides, tracks, and stops. It is the single most transformative upgrade you can make to your vehicle. For more than 110 years, Cooper tires have catered to drivers who look past the showroom floor and seek out products that overdeliver on performance, capability, and long-term durability.And that level of purpose-built engineering is more vital than ever. As vehicles grow heavier and more capable, tires need to do more than simply roll down an interstate. They have to withstand heavy payload demands, sudden weather changes, and unpredictable pavement. Cooper tires are built to that benchmark. Rooted in American engineering and real-world development, Cooper tires are built to an uncompromising standard that live up to their promises. From the rock-crawling STT Pro to the severe-snow-designated Stronghold AT, the Discoverer® family has earned its reputation through real-world testing from Alaskan ice to jagged mountain trails.Civilized on the Highway, Built for the PayloadThe new Cooper Discoverer® HT adapts that rugged all-terrain lineage for long-distance highway cruising, matching heavy-duty capability with quiet, refined composure. While it retains the structural durability to wander down a gravel trail with a trailer in tow, its core mission is maximizing comfort and control across hundreds of miles of open road.Cooper Discoverer® HTWhere many highway tires trade load capability for a soft ride, the Discoverer® HT is engineered to handle both. Straight, reinforced sidewalls provide the structural foundation needed to maintain an optimal contact patch under load. Whether the vehicle is running light or carrying family, gear, and tongue weight, the tire resists deformation, ensuring consistent steering response and predictable roadholding grip in any condition. It’s engineered for drivers whose tires have to hold their own—providing a dependable, hard-working partner that won’t fold when the truck or SUV is pushed to its limit.Engineered for the Job, Not Just the Showroom FloorCooper tires also tackle truck and SUV tire performance, with advanced features. Its proprietary 3-D Micro-Gauge Siping incorporates interlocking zig-zag sipes inside the tread blocks. Under heavy braking, sharp turns, or loaded acceleration, these interlocking sipes lock together to stiffen the tread block, to help support responsiveness. Crucially, these sipes run deep into the tread rubber, ensuring that gripping edges are still present to help with traction. That structural integrity backs up an exceptional UTQG treadwear rating of 720 and a 70,000-mile limited treadwear warranty on passenger fitments.Cooper Discoverer® HTThis is the tire for drivers who expect their trucks or suvs to show up for the long haul. Whether that means towing a camper into the backcountry, handling moving-day payloads, or eating up cross-country interstate miles in quiet comfort, the mission remains the same: a single set of tires that balances real-world traction, refined manners, and hard-working capability.To fit that wide spectrum of work, Cooper offers the Discoverer® HT across 19 passenger sizes covering 16- to 22-inch wheels (with section widths from 245 to 285 mm), alongside 16 light-truck (LT) options engineered with deeper tread grooves and higher load ratings. Backed by a 45-day satisfaction guarantee and over a century of research and development, the Discoverer® HT delivers what Cooper has always stood for: the quiet confidence that the job was done right.Find out more about the Cooper Discoverer® HT on Coopertire.com or visit your local tire shop retailer.

f9q409.title: Anthropic Shares Pop, Then Pull Back In Volatile Debut As AI Giant Goes Public
f9q409.content:
Anthropic shares jumped over 30% in the first minutes of trade at their Nasdaq debut before backtracking as the AI pioneer splashed down with the largest ever initial public offering in corporate history.

The first publicly traded, pure play AI company priced its hotly anticipated IPO last night at $83 a share, well above the $70 to $78 range initially anticipated, and valuing the company at $1.5 trillion. It opened just before noon Thursday up 30% at about $111, pushing its market value to $2 trillion, before ascending to $115. The stock, listed under the ticker symbol ANT, then skidded to $95 rose, and dipped again. Shares are currently changing hands at about $95, still above where the IPO priced, but also well off their highs.

The listing is seen as a litmus test of investor sentiment on the AI sector, which has taken its lumps lately amid heavy spending, a string of outages across sectors, growing public pushback on data centers, safety and jobs, and the ouster of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang from the company he founded.

The IPO raised more than $107 billion, the largest capital raise at an initial public offering on record, ahead of Elon Musk SpaceX’s $86 billion in June. The base deal covered 825 million Class A shares, some 800 million from the seven co-founders, with a $26 billion private placement layered on top.

Anthropic CEO and co-founder Dario Amodei with top executives and investors rang the opening bell at Nasdaq headquarters in Times Square Thursday with the image beamed onto a jumbotron on the building’s façade. Below, a crowd of onlookers, media and protestors gathered. Signage at the modest #StopTechOligarchs demonstration said the IPO endangered workers pension funds and the global economy and noted the company’s own language citing potentially catastrophic risk of AI.

In a note last night, Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co., called the $83 a share pricing “a clean read on demand: investors wanted exposure to a frontier lab at scale and the pricing reflects it, following SpaceX five months ago as the second core tech stalwart of this cycle to reach the public markets, and we expect OpenAI to follow in 2027.”

The sector “is going through a very turbulent, white-knuckle period,” he acknowledged. But “that does not change our longer-term view that $3 trillion to $4 trillion of capex will be spent over the next few years on the AI Revolution, and this sets the stage for the next phase of tech and infrastructure investment with Anthropic a central player in the buildout. phase of tech and infrastructure investment with Anthropic a central player in the buildout.”

1xti1bj.title: THR Celebrates Hollywood’s New Wave of Stars at Next Gen Dinner
1xti1bj.content:
Raise a glass for the next generation.

The Hollywood Reporter hosted its Next Gen dinner, presented by Meta, on Wednesday night, celebrating the magazine’s recent lists of fast-rising stars everyone is fighting to cast and 35 rising Hollywood executives under 35 on the rooftop of the new Public West Hollywood.

Sophie Nélisse, Charlie Hall and Keyla Monterroso Mejia came out to represent this year’s Next Gen talent group, alongside Widow’s Bay‘s Kingston Rumi Southwick, The Pitt‘s Supriya Ganesh and The Body stars Shirley Chen, Sofia Wylie, Kristina Bogic, Geena Meszaros, Sara Boustany and Bella Neuspiel (plus creator Quinn Shephard and showrunner Gina Gammell).

The evening began with cocktails and mingling on the roof, with Nélisse, Hall and Mejia taking a moment to pose together with their individual covers. Guests also stopped by the Meta Ray-Ban glasses try-on station, with each attendee receiving a pair that they could set up on the spot.

Sophie Nélisse, Charlie Hall and Keyla Monterroso Mejia

Rodin Eckenroth/The Hollywood Reporter via Getty Images

Kingston Rumi Southwick and Caylee Cowan

Savion Washington/The Hollywood Reporter via Getty Images

After some tray-passed apps and plenty of red carpet photos, everyone found their seats for the dinner portion of the evening. THR senior entertainment reporter Mia Galuppo offered up some brief remarks, telling the group how “we started this issue over 30 years ago with the idea that we are going to tap the future leaders of Hollywood,” with Donna Langley, Kevin Feige and Ari Emanuel among that early Next Gen exec crop. For the last decade THR has also done the in-front-of-the-camera list, as Galuppo noted, “It’s something that we take very seriously. We base it on our own tastes as well as our reporting, talking to executives in the industry about who they’re excited about and who audiences are excited about.”

Claudine Cazian, director of strategic partnerships at Meta, noted the company wanted “to highlight and spotlight together the freshest faces and the boldest voices that are reshaping the industry” and joked “looking around this room tonight, I am both energized and inspired and slightly jealous of the collagen in everybody’s cheekbones. Appreciate it while you have it — it goes, my friends.”

“What you do and what you give to all of us, it opens hearts, it opens minds, and what you do is push culture forward and that’s not easy to do,” she continued. “Sometimes it can even be scary, so we want to thank you collectively for your craft, for your time, for your energy, for your talent and for your voice,” as the guests raised their glasses. The evening capped with dinner — featuring portobello mushroom bolognese and citrus chile braised beef short ribs as the main dishes — and more conversation, with Caylee Cowan, Jessica Belkin, John Owen Lowe, celebrity groomer Aika Flores, Abubakr Ali, Milo Callaghan, Yasmeen Fletcher, Laëtitia Hollard, Madison Iseman and Lilah Pate rounding out the guest list.

The Body‘s Shirley Chen, Sofia Wylie, Kristina Bogic, Geena Meszaros, Sara Boustany and Bella Neuspiel

s9c5eu.title: Google gives Gemini the ability to use your Mac for you
s9c5eu.content:
Google on Thursday announced that it is bringing computer use to its Gemini desktop application on macOS, allowing its AI to complete tasks on users’ behalf, navigating native Mac apps, and browsing websites in the background.

The tech giant is a little late to the game with this launch, as other leading AI model makers like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta have already been offering agentic features in their desktop applications for some time. Meanwhile, Google only this week announced the broader rollout of Gemini’s “Tasks,” the in-app feature that allows the AI to work more as an agent, helping users sign into websites, make online purchases, or book appointments.

Google also only recently began admitting early testers to try its revamped “CC” AI agent, announced in September, which is designed to help families stay organized across email, calendars, chats, and tasks.

Computer use is another type of agentic offering that allows an AI agent to take actions directly on the user’s computer — in Gemini’s case, a Mac. This allows the AI to complete multi-step tasks that involve getting things done across the local files, apps, and the web. After the user instructs the AI what they want to do, they’ll see the agent working in a live preview in their chat, while still keeping their screen and cursor free to continue working on other things.

As with other AI agents offering computer use, users can pause, stop, and approve Gemini’s actions before they happen.

Google suggests the feature could be useful for tedious tasks and other workflows, like filling out forms, repeating the same task over and over across a batch of files, organizing files into folders based on specific criteria, creating slideshows from files or information in online dashboards, and more.

The feature is initially available in English in the U.S. and requires the Gemini app for Mac and a Google AI Plus, Pro, or Ultra subscription. The company didn’t say when it would expand to other markets or platforms.

1gzku5u.title: New Baldur’s Gate 3 console mods include spells, and another difficulty mode
1gzku5u.content: A new batch of Baldur’s Gate 3 mods has been approved for release on console.As noted by the Baldur’s Gate 3 modding subreddit, 12 new mods have been approved and can now be downloaded on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S, having previously been available exclusively on PC.The new mods range from cosmetic to sweeping gameplay changes, including a brand new difficulty setting to choose from.Baldur’s Gate 3 console mods approved on November 19Life Drain Spell (Larloch’s Minor Drain): A new level 1 necromancy spellIllithid Powers Per Combat:  – Illithid Powers are now per combatAoman Head Preset: A new head to choose from if you’re playing as an elfHalsin’s Gift: Wooden Duck Earrings: New earrings in the character creatorHoly Avenger Set: Two new weaponsDrow Leather Boots for Minthara: Armour redesign for MintharaBerry’s Vitrinelle – Couture Jewellery Collection: New wearable jewelleryIncreased Boss Health: Makes boss battles harder by giving them more healthBrutal Difficulty: A new difficulty built on top of Tactician in the base gameGrab It (Auto Loot / Apportation): Automatically picks up loot so you don’t have to select every individual objectStarlight Crew Dice: New dice cosmeticsPermanent Blessings of Shar: Makes several Shar-related blessings permanentWhile these mods have been available on PC for some time, the process of getting them on console is much longer. Mod authors must submit their creations for approval to make sure they will work on console and fit Larian‘s guidelines. New batches of mods tend to be approved once a week.Mods can be installed from a menu on the title screen, which takes you to an in-game mod page powered by mod.io.Console mods were added to Baldur’s Gate 3 as part of a path in 2024. While more limited than the offerings on PC, it finally gave console players the chance to download fan-made cosmetics and gameplay tweaks. It was a natural fit for a community that quickly attracted a modding scene, even when the game was in early access prior to 2023.

gh-1410247473.title: GitHub - robongrui/derp: Doom Engine Remaster Project (DERP) — an enhanced / experimental Doom source port featuring dynamic lighting, weather simulation, physics, reflections and more.
gh-1410247473.content:
A few thoughts
The technically correct name would be Remaster Project for DOOM Engine
Games, but RPFDE is a terrible acronym, so DERP it is. Up to v0.4.5 the
project was called Duct-Tape DOOM.
It has grown well past what I first had in mind. The original idea is
described further down and still holds. Along the way I found that what I
enjoy most is working out what these places were meant to look and feel like,
and what the hardware of the time kept them from doing.
My work on Doom, Doom II and Heretic is opinionated. I try to add only what
the original maps, artwork or game logic already suggest, and then take those
hints seriously.
I treat DERP as a creative project. Code is one of the tools I use to build
it. I'm glad to hear whether it works, whether it's fun and whether it does
what it sets out to do. How much of the code I typed myself is a different
question, and one the project isn't trying to answer.
DERP is a hobby project and development happens privately. The public
repository holds the versions I choose to release, without my ongoing
experiments or unfinished work. I sometimes show upcoming features on
YouTube; they reach the repository when I'm ready to release them.
Forks and contributions
The GPL gives you every right to fork DERP, and I respect that. If you mainly
want to fix bugs, improve performance or extend existing features, I'd prefer
a pull request to another distribution of essentially the same project.
Improvements developed together reach more people.
What this is
An idea of how DOOM could have looked if id had kept iterating on this engine,
and if we still played on CRTs. It tries to look newer without looking modern.
Under the hood it is a port of id Software's 1997 DOOM source release to
Windows, macOS and Linux, with an optional GPU renderer that builds a 3D scene
from the loaded WAD while the game runs.
Everything the renderer adds is worked out from the original artwork, maps and
game state. It needs no replacement textures, models, authored lighting or
edited maps, so vanilla and limit-removing WADs get the effects without their
authors preparing anything. Sound works the same way. Every sound DOOM didn't
have, from a lamp's buzz to a window breaking, is synthesized by code when the
game starts, and where it plays is read from the map. The exceptions are
listed where they come up: one spoken word, the voices and cries of DERP
mode's monsters (generated with ElevenLabs), the kick's leg and the kneeling
soldiers' frames (generated with ChatGPT), the bundled SoundFont, and recorded soundtracks you supply
yourself.
Most effects are fake-modern: cheap tricks of the kind I liked in late-90s
games, chosen over the techniques a modern engine would use. Effects stay or
go based on how they look in the game, and the code is written for trying
ideas out quickly. It isn't meant as a reference engine or a library. I'd be
glad if some of the ideas end up in other projects.
Claude writes much of the code. I decide what DERP should do and how it should
look and sound, test the results in the game, and keep iterating until they
match what I had in mind. Without that workflow I wouldn't have the spare time
for a project like this.
The defaults are how I like to play. Nearly everything can be changed in the
settings panel, F4.
At a glance

3D renderer on SDL_gpu: Vulkan on Windows and Linux, Metal on macOS.
Native resolution, any aspect ratio, mouse look and free aim, movement
interpolated between game tics, optional MSAA and HDR output.
Classic renderer: the original 320×200 software view is one setting away.
No asset pack: the WAD's own textures, flats, sprites and palettes are
the source material.
Compatibility: vanilla and limit-removing maps with DEHACKED patches.
SIGIL plays as episode 5 of The Ultimate DOOM.
Three ways to play: Normal is DOOM's own game with DERP's look. DERP
mode, the default, is where the experiments live: monsters that take cover
and talk, a player who can crouch, slide and kick, slow motion that costs
something, and DOOM's first episode at night in the rain. Phobos plays the
first episode on a moon 22 km across, in vacuum.
Light: the level is lit as one model by its own lamps, screens, windows
and the light bouncing off them, baked when the level loads and re-baked
when doors open or lamps get shot out. Monsters block light and cast real
shadows.
Climate and weather: rain, snow, sand, ash, fog, dry ice, nukage rain or
a firestorm, at any hour, temperature and wind. The map's rooms are worked
out at load, the wind blows through them, and blasts, footsteps and doors
disturb what falls and lies.
Window glass that reflects and shatters, lights that can be shot
out, lamps that blink with DOOM's flickering sectors.
Combat: wound holes that follow the animation, blood that runs down
steps, ragdolls drawn back into sprites, gore, muzzle flashes and
explosions in four styles.
Skies with depth: painted mountains stand at their own distances, cloud
skies get volumetric clouds, Doom II's city becomes buildings.
Sound: room acoustics measured from the map, sound that finds its way
round corners and through doors, headphone output through a measured head,
and synthesized footsteps, sparks, breaking glass and ambience.
Music: a SoundFont synth with the bundled GeneralUser GS bank, an OPL FM
synth written from the chip's manual, the Mac's system synth, or recorded
soundtracks (PlayStation, 3DO, the 2024 re-release's) from packs you own.
Heretic runs as a second program on the same renderer and sound,
tuned for its fantasy world.
Controls: gamepads, gyro aim, rumble, rebinding, the Steam Deck.
For mappers: a DERPINFO lump sets a map's weather, wind, hour, sun,
distance fog and wall mirrors, or switches on Phobos physics. Other ports
ignore it.
Not supported: Boom, MBF21 and GZDoom maps, Hexen, DOOM 64, slopes, 3D
floors, model packs, ray tracing and multiplayer.

The Windows build gets the most testing. The macOS and Linux builds compile in
CI and have had less real play.
Download and play
Ready-to-play builds for Windows, macOS and Linux are on the
Releases page. Each includes
Freedoom, so it plays straight away.
Start the launcher: DERP.exe on Windows, derp on Linux, Play
DERP.app on the Mac. It lists the game WADs it finds in the wads folder
next to it, in DOOMWADDIR and DOOMWADPATH, and in DOOM and Heretic games
installed through Steam or GOG. Drop files on its window and each goes where
it belongs: game WADs to the games list, custom WADs and .deh/.bex patches
to the load list, soundtrack packs to the music, .sf2 files to the
SoundFont. Its Settings page has the same options as F4. It works with a
gamepad.
PLAY.md has the controls and more on the launcher and options.
The ambience is off by default (F4 → Sound → Made-up sounds), and quiet on
purpose when on; the music covers most of it. To hear the soundscape, turn the
music down or off in Options → Sound Volume.
Ways to play
F4 → Game → World → Gameplay picks one of three. Switching restarts a
first-episode map; you keep what you carry.
Normal
DOOM's own game. Every map looks the way DERP derives it from the WAD, sun and
all, and the rules are id's.
DERP mode
The default, and where most of the experiments go. It is unfinished: parts are
rough, some are half-built, and any of it may change or go away between
releases. Its rules apply on the maps id made and are off in demos and
netgames.
Monsters that think. Soldiers work as squads with jobs. They take cover
behind the map's corners, kneel behind low walls and stand to fire over them,
move one at a time while the others cover, hold doorways, guard keys,
switches and the pickups they were placed around, and fall back or set
ambushes after a lost fight. Word spreads: a soldier who hears gunfire or sees
a friend leave readies the room. A director keeps the pressure in check and
backs off when you are picking them off. Imps hunt as a pack: one holds your
attention while another goes round, they climb, hop across nukage, jump
through any window they fit (shattering the glass), and some hang from the
ceiling in dark corners and drop on your back. Pinkies smell you and charge.
Skill levels change how sharply they aim and how fast they spot you.
-derpai turns the AI on in any mode, for testing.
Monsters that talk. Soldiers shout what they are doing, pass on what they
know, chat when they think they are alone, and die mid-sentence. Each keeps
its own voice. Imps hiss and screech. The cries, pain and death sounds ship
with the game in derp-cries.wad; the spoken lines are a separate download,
derp-voices.wad, placed beside the game WAD. Without it the soldiers only
cry out.
A player with legs. You run at Quake's pace, 320 units a second, a
little over half of Doomguy's 583, so monsters that walk at a man's pace have
a fair chance. C crouches, and crouching out of a run slides. E is a
low jump and Q a kick; out of a slide the kick becomes a sweep. Kicked
soldiers go down and get up again with a kip-up. With Gore on, a severed head
can be kicked about too.
Slow motion that costs. The hourglass beside the status bar holds four
charges. It runs down while the world is slow, a kill refills half a charge,
and a headshot or a kill while sliding refills a whole one. The right mouse
button is the shootslide: a slide out of a run into slow motion for one charge.
See Slow motion.
Heads. Shots hit the head where the current frame draws it. A pistol
headshot kills quietly and the victim doesn't cry out.
Guns with jobs. Bullets have their own speed, spread and falloff per gun,
and a round that kills carries on through the body.
Looks picked by hand. DOOM's first episode lies at night in a downpour,
with some windows broken before you arrive. See
Rain, night and wear.
Rooms that ring as built. Room tails are traced from the map's real walls
at level start, and far rooms are heard ringing through their doorways. See
Room tails traced from the map.
Phobos
DOOM's first episode says it takes place on Phobos, a moon of Mars 22 km
across. Pick Phobos and the episode plays as if that were literally true.
It touches only the first episode (DOOM's or Freedoom: Phase 1's) and never
runs in demos or netgames.
Phobos pulls at 1/1700 of Earth's gravity, so walking doesn't work. Movement
keys give gentle hops that float for about twenty seconds, Use next to a wall
pushes you off along the floor, E jumps, and running fires the suit's
thrusters. Knockback and recoil are real; a barrel is 225 kg of
monopropellant. Every sector has an air pressure and air rushes out through
every opening: doors cycle as airlocks, a broken window vents a room, and
whatever isn't held down goes with the draft, monsters included. Outside is
vacuum under a black sky with Mars in it, and you and your rockets can climb
to about 900 m. Grav boots let you walk on ceilings, and Guns turn you
spins you into backflips.
F4 → Game → Phobos sets how much help you get (legs and guns only,
thrusters, or thrusters with grav boots), whether monsters wear mag boots,
and how hard decompression pulls. Mappers can switch Phobos on for their own
maps with phobos = true in DERPINFO.
See linuxdoom-1.10/p_phobos.c and
linuxdoom-1.10/p_boots.c.
Heretic
DERP plays Raven's Heretic on the same 3D renderer, lighting, sound and music,
again worked out from the WAD. Pick a Heretic WAD in the launcher and it
starts the Heretic program, derp-heretic, which ships next to the DOOM one.
You need your own copy: the 2025 Heretic + Hexen release has both the new
heretic.wad and the original DOS HERETIC.WAD, and both work.
The effects are tuned for a fantasy world. There is no window glass and there
are no lamps to shoot out. The Torch item is the light you carry, burning as a
flickering flame, and the hero light is on faintly by default. Torches,
chandeliers and serpent statues light their rooms, stained glass glints and
throws its colours onto the floor, water is clear and mirror-like, the Ice
Grotto's floor gets glassy streaks, and gloss comes from each texture's
material. Episodes 4 and 5 get skies of their own: hanging tendrils that move
one by one, and dead trees in fog. Where Heretic already has a sound of its
own, such as its wind and waterfalls, the game's sound is used and DERP's is
left off.
Heretic has had far less play than DOOM. heretic/README.md
has its controls and what does and doesn't work yet.
SIGIL
With The Ultimate DOOM loaded, John Romero's SIGIL (E5M1–E5M9) plays as
episode 5, with its own names, intermission and menu entry. Bring your own
SIGIL.wad.
Episode 0.5: SCP_7179_B
It's in the episode menu when you play DOOM II, TNT or Plutonia, and it is the
one place where DERP brings a map of its own. That is all this README says
about it. scp_7179_b/README.md has how to start it
and the credits.
Screenshots

The settings panel
F4 opens the settings over the paused game. Options are sorted into four
groups (Game, Controls, Graphics and Sound), each with tabs, and the
highlighted option's description is shown at the bottom. Options that only
refine another are greyed out while it is off.
Options that cost frame time carry bars: one green, two yellow, three red,
measured on E1M1 and E1M2. Options that cost only in some places say where
(near windows, near liquids, under open sky, in fights). F4 →
Graphics → Display → Preset sets all of them at once and leaves matters of
taste alone:

Preset
For

Lowest
Old or built-in graphics chips. Bump detail, bloom, fog, sky depth, reflections and monster shadows off; the light itself stays.

Handheld
The Steam Deck. Bloom, texel-aligned light and glass reflections off; monsters fall procedurally instead of as ragdolls.

Balanced
DERP as it comes.

High
Balanced with 2× anti-aliasing.

Everything
4× anti-aliasing and half-resolution liquid reflections.

Show FPS under Display has five levels. Full shows a frame-time graph,
CPU load, how frames reach the screen, the GPU, the version, the map and what
each running system costs, so a screenshot (F7) says what a bug report needs.
Full, with GPU times adds the GPU time of each part of the picture; it
waits on each part, so the game runs slower while it shows. The key left of
1 steps through the levels while you play.
Settings are saved in graphics.cfg. Each option's key is listed beside it in
platform/settings_panel.cpp.
What the graphics do
Light comes from things that look like lights
DOOM hints at its lighting through sector brightness, glowing textures and
flats, decorations, windows and the shapes of rooms. The renderer turns those
hints into light sources.
Lamp strips, computer panels, lava and other glowing artwork are recognised by
texture name and palette colour. Their bright pixels become glow masks and
light sources. Wall panels shine mostly forward, so they don't light through
their own wall, and lamps close by light the walls beside them at a raking
angle. Computer walls dotted with a few LEDs light the room only as much as
those LEDs would. Torches, candles and other glowing decorations cast light
sized to their artwork.
A lamp lights as strongly as its sector's light level says. The level is the
mapper's stand-in for the lamp's brightness, so a strip set only a notch above
its room stays a dim fixture: the strength rises with the square of the level,
from nothing at 96 to full at 208. Floor paint the mapper lit like a fixture,
such as FLOOR1_6, glows too.
Windows and other openings to the sky let the outdoor light in. A barrel's
slime glows on top.

See
platform/scene3d/bake_lights.cpp,
platform/emissive.h and
platform/surface_lighting.h.
The whole level is lit as one model
F4 → Graphics → Lighting → Lighting offers two models.
Whole level, the default, lights the level by its own lights: lamps,
screens, windows, the sky and what bounces off them, each reaching as far as
real light does. DOOM's sector light levels no longer light the rooms. Light
spills from a bright room into the dark one next door, daylight reaches into
rooms through their openings, and a room whose lamps are shot out goes black.
It is still being built and is finished only for indoor areas so far.
Two sliders tune it. Surfaces return light sets how much light a surface
bounces on. DOOM's textures are painted dark, as if already in dim light, so
taken as drawn a floor returns about a quarter and bounce dies at once; the
default counts them twice as light. Fill light lets a room its own lights
don't reach keep some of the light level its mapper gave it. It is off by
default. Light by logic is a test that ignores the mapper's light levels
entirely: every lamp shines in full by its artwork and daylight follows the
hour.
Classic is DOOM's own light level per sector with the baked lamps,
windows and bounce on top. It has its own options for spilling light through
doorways, darkening rooms that their lamps light well (so the light seems to
come from the lamps), and tinting a room by the colour of its bounced lamp
light.
See platform/scene3d/light_rooms.cpp,
platform/scene3d/room_fill.cpp and
platform/scene3d/bake_bounce.cpp.
Static light is baked when a level loads
The bake works on DOOM's 2D map and is far simpler than a modern lightmap.
It gathers light from lamps, glowing textures and liquids, decorations,
windows and the sky, with walls and closed portals blocking it. It adds
bounce, sky fill, sun shadows, ambient occlusion in corners and under ledges,
and shadows from decorations such as columns, trees and hanging bodies. The
result is snapped to the texture grid, so the light changes in steps of DOOM
texels.
Each wall texel and floor cell also stores the direction its light comes from,
in the way Half-Life 2 stored it. With Bumps in all baked light on, seams,
bricks and panel edges catch the baked light from the side it comes from and
fall into shade on the other.
Baking is fast enough to repeat. It runs on the graphics card by default (on a
Mac, whose processor is quicker at it, on the processor), stages whose inputs
haven't changed are taken from a cache on disk, and Quick sky and bounce
bakes trades a little evenness for several seconds on big outdoor maps.

See
platform/baked_lighting.h,
platform/scene3d/bake_basis.cpp,
platform/scene3d/bake_cache.cpp and
platform/scene3d/relight.cpp.
Light changes during play
Doors, lifts and lowering walls spill light through as they move. A door that
stays open, or a floor lowered for good, gets its light baked again in the
background once it stops. Doors that close again keep the spill only.
A lamp that is shot out takes its light with it. With Shot-out light at
once, the lamps near you are pre-baked as if already broken on helper
threads, so the room darkens on the frame the lamp breaks. It costs 50–150 MB
of memory. Quick uses three threads; Gentle uses two and dips the
frame rate about half as much. Re-bakes run on the graphics card by default,
or on the processor on a Steam Deck or a Mac.
A muzzle flash, a spark or an exploding barrel briefly lifts the light of the
room it goes off in, including the far side of a pillar but not the room next
door (Flashes light the room).
Eye adaptation meters the picture: a dim room opens up and its windows
burn out, and daylight reins it in.
Hero light (Off, Faint or Strong; off by default in DOOM) lifts what is
close to you and nearly black by a few steps, so you can make out walls and
monsters in the dark. Rooms lit by their own lights don't change, and nothing
shines, casts a shadow or glints from it.
See platform/scene3d/relight.cpp,
platform/scene3d/shot_lights.cpp,
platform/scene3d/room_pulse.cpp and
platform/scene3d/exposure.cpp.

gh-1405928460.title: GitHub - Polocop/genewars: GWRecomp v1.2: Gene Wars (Bullfrog, 1996) as a native Win32/SDL2 program, statically recompiled from your own GW.EXE (1.1 patch). English/Spanish launcher, six game languages, widescreen, Zoom Out, 120 FPS, CD music. No game files included.
gh-1405928460.content:
GWRecomp — Gene Wars, natively on Windows

Mission 1 (Exceland) in widescreen 854×480: an extractor on the GOOP field, the next one being placed, animated sea

GWRecomp runs Gene Wars (Bullfrog Productions, 1996, version 1.1) as a native Win32 program, without DOSBox.
The original x86-32 DOS4GW executable is statically lifted to C and runs on a modern host layer (SDL2 video, audio
and input, DOS/DPMI services, a virtual Sound Blaster for the game's own Miles mixer, CD-DA playback). The game logic,
AI and mixer are the original code; the host only replaces the hardware and DOS around it.
It needs your own copy of Gene Wars 1.1: no game files are included (see Legal).
Download: latest release (GWRecomp-*-win32.zip, Windows,
ready to play with your own GENEWARS folder) · Descarga: última versión.
Screenshots

Zoom Out: the 1152×640 map canvas at 0.87×, sharp scaling
Classic 640×480, as in 1996

Native launcher (English / Spanish): start, continue, start-up options
Missions: pick any of the 24 missions

Graphics: view mode, resolution, 60/120 FPS, filter, water and GOOP
The original planet-system screen, with its sounds

The source lives in gwrecomp/. This repository started as a fork of
mefistotelis/genewars and is now a standalone project; that unfinished
engine re-implementation, with its history, stays in the source folders of this repository, untouched. Earlier
GitHub issues are kept in gwrecomp/docs/issues-archive.md.
Features

Native Win32/SDL2 build of the original executable: one gwrecomp.exe plus SDL2.dll, no DOSBox, no emulator.
Deterministic regression check: the A/B suite renders 56 frame captures at four points of mission 1 (after
the landing, before a creature is ready, during construction, extractor selected) and compares them with reference
hashes; v1.2 matches all 56 bit for bit. The presentation extras (interpolation, water, audio) never write game
memory, so they cannot change these frames.
Three view modes:

Classic 640×480 (the original frame),
Widescreen 854×480,
Zoom Out on a 1152×640 map canvas (wheel zoom 0.87×–2×, Home returns to 1×).

Sharp scaling to any window or monitor: supersampled sharp-bilinear (pixel interiors stay solid, only the seams
blend), exact nearest when the window is a whole multiple; F7 switches sharp / EPX / CRT.
120 FPS presentation with camera scroll interpolation; the simulation keeps the game's own tick rate.
Animated water and GOOP: sea ripples and drifting glints, soft highlights on GOOP, on ground pixels only and in
the presented frame only (units, buildings and HUD are never touched).
Complete audio:

Smacker video sound,
the original Miles sound effects through a virtual SB16,
automatic CD-DA music from your own .cue image,
stereo panning and distance fade calibrated to the visible map width,
subtle ±4.5 % pitch variation on effects (never on voices),
music ducking while a voice speaks.

Native graphical launcher in English and Spanish (ES / EN buttons; by default it follows the Windows
language): mission selector 1–24, Continue, view/resolution/filter/audio options, all saved in gwrecomp.ini.

Installation (English)

Version check. GWRecomp is built on the GW.EXE of the official 1.1 patch (built 26 Nov 1996). The European
CD itself, and the common "Genewars (Europe) (En,Fr,De,Es,It,Sv)" image, carry the original 1.0 GW.EXE (built
2 Sep 1996, 1,265,994 bytes), which GWRecomp refuses ("GW.EXE is not the Gene Wars 1.1 one..."): install the game
from the CD and apply the 1.1 patch first. Installs in English, French, German, Italian, Spanish or Swedish are
accepted (speech files of the six languages are known). Only the Spanish 1.1 TEXT.DAT has been seen so far; the
other languages' 1.1 TEXT.DAT is accepted when it has the 1.1 layout (627 texts), and that case has not been tested
with a real installation yet.

Have Gene Wars 1.1 (European edition) installed: the GENEWARS folder created by the original installer
(DATA, LEVELS, SOUND, INTRO, ANIMS, LDATA, S, SPEECH, SAVE and the loose files such as GW.EXE).
GWRecomp checks them with SHA-256 and only reads them.
Download GWRecomp-v1.2-win32.zip from Releases and unzip it anywhere you can write (saves and logs go next to the program).
Double-click gwrecomp.exe. In the launcher press CHANGE and choose your GENEWARS folder; the four marks
DATA / LEVELS / SOUND / INTRO turn green. The ES / EN buttons at the top switch the launcher's language.
Start the game, continue the last game, or pick a mission.

"Windows protected your PC": gwrecomp.exe is not code-signed, so Windows SmartScreen may stop it the first
time. Click More info → Run anyway. If Windows blocks the downloaded zip as a whole, right-click it before
unzipping → Properties → tick Unblock → OK. You can check the file against the SHA-256 published with
each release.
First start: the first time you enter the game, gwrecomp.exe prepares two files in work\ from your GW.EXE
(checked by SHA-256). It takes a moment and happens once. Those files come from your copy of the game: do not share
them.
gwrecomp.ini (the launcher writes it; gwrecomp.ini.example documents every key):

Key
Meaning

mode
classic, widescreen or zoomout

resolution, fullscreen
window size (auto, 1080p, 1440p, 2160p, WxH), borderless fullscreen

fps
presentation rate, 60 or 120

filter
sharp, epx or crt (also F7 in game)

water_effects
animated water and GOOP (1/0)

enhanced_audio
calibrated panning, pitch variation, music ducking (1/0)

language
launcher language: en, es or auto (Windows display language)

cd_cue
path to your own Gene Wars CD image .cue, for the CD music (launcher: PLAY → CD IMAGE)

data_dir
your GENEWARS folder (the launcher fills it in)

In game: F7 filter, F8 turbo 1×/2×/4×, mouse wheel zoom, Home zoom 1×, F10 release the mouse, WASD / arrows / middle
button scroll the map, ESC game options.
Building from source (Windows, MSYS2 mingw32, Python, LLVM clang) is described in
gwrecomp/README.md and gwrecomp/tools/rebuild/README_BUILD.md.
Instalación (español)

Comprueba la versión. GWRecomp está hecho sobre el GW.EXE del parche oficial 1.1 (compilado el 26/11/1996).
El CD europeo, y la imagen habitual «Genewars (Europe) (En,Fr,De,Es,It,Sv)», traen el GW.EXE original 1.0
(02/09/1996, 1.265.994 bytes), que GWRecomp rechaza («GW.EXE no es el de Gene Wars 1.1…»): instala el juego desde el
CD y aplica antes el parche 1.1. Se aceptan instalaciones en inglés, francés, alemán, italiano, español o sueco.
Del TEXT.DAT 1.1 solo se conoce el español; el de los demás idiomas se acepta si tiene el formato 1.1 (627
textos), y ese caso aún no se ha probado con una instalación real.

Ten instalado Gene Wars 1.1 (edición europea): la carpeta GENEWARS que crea el instalador original
(DATA, LEVELS, SOUND, INTRO, ANIMS, LDATA, S, SPEECH, SAVE y los archivos sueltos como GW.EXE).
GWRecomp los comprueba con SHA-256 y solo los lee.
Descarga GWRecomp-v1.2-win32.zip de Releases y descomprímelo en una carpeta donde puedas escribir (ahí se guardan partidas y registros).
Haz doble clic en gwrecomp.exe. En el lanzador pulsa CAMBIAR y elige tu carpeta GENEWARS; las cuatro
marcas DATA / LEVELS / SOUND / INTRO se ponen en verde. Los botones ES / EN de arriba cambian el idioma del
lanzador.
Inicia el juego, continúa la última partida o elige una misión.

«Windows protegió su PC»: gwrecomp.exe no está firmado digitalmente, así que SmartScreen puede detenerlo la
primera vez. Pulsa Más información → Ejecutar de todas formas. Si Windows bloquea el zip descargado, antes de
descomprimirlo haz clic derecho → Propiedades → marca Desbloquear → Aceptar. Puedes comprobar el archivo
con el SHA-256 que se publica en cada versión.
Primer arranque: la primera vez que entras al juego, gwrecomp.exe prepara dos archivos en work\ a partir de
tu GW.EXE (comprobado por SHA-256). Tarda un momento y solo ocurre una vez. Salen de tu copia del juego: no los
compartas.
Opciones: todo lo que cambias en el lanzador se guarda en gwrecomp.ini (modo de vista, resolución, pantalla
completa, 60/120 FPS, filtro, water_effects, enhanced_audio, language = es / en / auto). Para la música del CD, en la pestaña
JUGAR pulsa IMAGEN DEL CD y elige el .cue de tu propia imagen del CD (se guarda como cd_cue). gwrecomp.ini.example explica cada clave.
Legal
Gene Wars is © Bullfrog Productions / Electronic Arts. GWRecomp is unaffiliated with and unendorsed by the rights
holders.

This repository contains no game executable, data, video, audio, disc image or extracted game code. It contains
the host layer, the lifter and the tools that translate your GW.EXE at build time, plus a few screenshots in
gwrecomp/docs/screenshots/ that show the game's graphics for illustration only.
A built gwrecomp.exe is that translation compiled: it contains native code derived from the original Gene
Wars program. It contains none of the game's data (graphics, sounds, videos, levels, speech), which are always read
from your own GENEWARS folder. Whether a prebuilt binary may be redistributed is a question for the rights
holders; this project does not grant any such right.
License of GWRecomp's own work: MIT. It covers the code, scripts and documentation written
for GWRecomp under gwrecomp/ (host layer, runtime, lifter, tools, launcher, build scripts). It does not cover,
and grants nothing over: Gene Wars itself or any code derived from GW.EXE (including the lifted code inside a
built gwrecomp.exe), the game's graphics in the screenshots, the original function names and the short residual
byte patterns listed in PROVENANCE.md, the upstream re-implementation in the other folders
(GPL-2.0-or-later, as stated in its file headers), or third-party material, which keeps its own license
(THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES; SDL2: zlib; pcrecomp patch: MIT; DOSBox-X patch: GPL-2.0).
