10gqqh0.title: Продажи Lada могут упасть: АВТОВАЗ ждет возвращения льготных кредитов
10gqqh0.content: Глава АВТОВАЗа Соколов: продажи Lada в ноябре могут упасть ниже 30 тыс. штукПродажи Lada в России по итогам ноября 2026 года рискуют оказаться ниже 30 тыс. штук. Такой сценарий вполне реален из-за завершения программ льготного автокредитования – об этом в кулуарах «Транспортной недели» журналистам рассказал глава АВТОВАЗа Максим Соколов.Стоит ли паниковать? На АВТОВАЗе, судя по всему, не спешат драматизировать. «АВТОВАЗ рассчитывает на восстановление продаж благодаря возобновлению льготного автокредитования в декабре, которое позволит удовлетворить отложенный спрос», – цитирует Соколова агентство. Проще говоря, часть покупателей не отказалась от машины, а просто сдвинула покупку до момента, когда господдержка снова заработает.Дальше в календаре – 2027 год: поправки к проекту федерального бюджета предусматривают увеличение финансирования льготного автокредитования. Правда, для автомобилей, которые участвуют в программе, прорабатывается изменение требований к локализации.Отдельная ставка – на обновление модельного ряда. Скажем, стартуют продажи Lada Vesta с новым 1,8-литровым двигателем; в компании рассчитывают, что свежие версии поддержат спрос.На большие объемы продаж нового кроссовера Lada Azimut в декабре 2026 года в «АВТОВАЗе» не рассчитывают. Выпуск после запуска производства будет расти постепенно, а определяющим для проекта Соколов назвал 2027 год.Итогами Lada Iskra к концу 2026-го АВТОВАЗ в целом удовлетворен. В семейство входят седан, универсал и кросс-универсал – их выпускают с различными сочетаниями двигателей и коробок передач.Про перемены в линейке Lada «За рулем» уже рассказывал, показывая первые живые фото обновленной Vesta с мотором 1.8.Понравилась публикация?Тогда добавьте «За рулем» в список интересных источников: 1. Откройте https://google.com... 2. Поставьте галочку напротив нашего изданияГотово – остаемся на связи! «За рулем» можно читать и в MAX

1ms18za.title: James Gray on Francis Ford Coppola’s Advice That Shaped His Career
1ms18za.content:
When filmmaker James Gray was a teenager, he wrote a fan letter to Francis Ford Coppola. To his surprise, the legendary filmmaker wrote back with a piece of advice that would come to shape Gray’s entire approach to cinema.

“He said, ‘Be personal, James. There’s only one of you in this world,’” Gray recalled during a press conference Sunday at the Doha Film Festival. “I’ve tried to take that to heart, that if I have anything to say at all, if I have a voice that matters at all, it’s best that I become as personal as I can.”

Decades later, that philosophy remains central to Gray’s filmmaking, even as he argues that the film industry increasingly pressures directors to suppress their individual voices.

“So much of the system, the systems in the cinema, both in the United States and abroad, try to discourage you from your own voice,” he said. “Or, if they don’t discourage you actively, they try to get you to bury your voice in a larger statement, or another form of genre, where it’s hidden.”

The director was in Doha to present the MENA premiere of “Paper Tiger,” his latest crime drama starring Adam Driver, Miles Teller and Scarlett Johansson. Set in 1980s New York, the film follows two brothers whose pursuit of the American Dream draws them into a dangerous scheme involving the Russian mafia.

Drawing heavily on his own family history, Gray described the film as an attempt to faithfully capture his father’s relationship with his uncle, while acknowledging the possible limitations of his own memory years later. He also recalled how a confrontation between his parents found its way into the film, with the actors recreating the incident almost exactly as it had unfolded in real life.

Although “Paper Tiger” is framed as a crime drama, Gray said he does not think of his films primarily in terms of genre, which he sees as a way of categorizing cinema rather than defining its true purpose.

“I’m just telling my story as best I can, as clearly as I can, as honestly as I can, and I hope for the best,” he said. For Gray, that commitment to honesty is also a means of fostering compassion and understanding. “That is how we extend the idea of compassion and sympathy in this world,” he explained. “Hopefully you can see something in me that matters to you.”

“I have been very lucky to be able to pursue a cinema which is very directly personal,” he added. “So I don’t take it lightly. It’s a responsibility I take very seriously. And I think it’s actually the true calling of the filmmaker.”

The conversation also turned to the future of independent cinema, with Brazilian producer Rodrigo Teixeira, whose “Paper Tiger” and “Furies” are both screening in Doha, pushing back against concerns about the dominance of Hollywood blockbusters.

“You’re always going to have space to create original films outside of the system, because it’s impossible to own the whole system, even with all these mergers,” Teixeira said, citing companies such as A24 and Neon as examples of how independent filmmaking continues to thrive.

Drawing a comparison between filmmaking in Brazil and the U.S., Teixeira argued that independent producers face much the same challenges regardless of geography. The principal difference, he said, is the public funding available in his home country, where federal support for cinema has long helped sustain the industry.

“We have a government who supports cinema, who supports art,” he said, contrasting Brazil’s system with the U.S., where comparable government support is absent.

Gray, meanwhile, recalled that he once believed cinema might follow the trajectory of opera, flourishing for roughly a century before eventually being eclipsed by another art form. While he acknowledged that cinema faces growing competition from video games and other forms of entertainment, and described the dominance of the blockbuster model as “overall quite harmful.” But the increasing accessibility of filmmaking technology has begun to challenge his earlier pessimism.

“I have a kind of optimism about the availability of technology and how that will introduce new voices.”

12ufo9p.title: SXSW Forges Partnership With Egypt's UTH Festival
12ufo9p.content:
Austin’s South by Southwest Film and TV Festival has forged a partnership with Egypt’s UTH Festival dedicated to youth culture under which UTH will become SXSW‘s partner in Egypt.

The agreement is aimed at “identifying emerging talent and building opportunities for Egyptian filmmakers, musicians, creators, founders and business leaders to engage with SXSW’s international network,” according to a statement.

The third edition of the just concluded UTH Festival just ran Nov. 20 and 21 at the Grand Egyptian Museum in Giza, on the west bank of the Nile opposite Cairo, attracting roughly 10,000 attendees, according to organizers. This year’s festival, held under the theme “Work in Progress,” covered fashion, design, creator economy, film, music, food and sports, among other spheres.

The announcement stems from an initiative bringing SXSW and Egyptian industry figures together during the UTH fest, which was attended by Peter Lewis, who is SXSW’s chief commercial officer.

As part of the collaboration, an Egyptian delegation comprising roughly 20 participants will travel to SXSW to attend the fest between March 13–21. Curated and led by UTH, the delegation will “bring together representatives from Egypt’s film and music industries, the creator economy, entrepreneurship, investment and institutional sectors,” according to the statement. The agreement also includes plans for “a UTH-led programming session and a community gathering in Austin,” the statement added.

The collaboration also envisions possible Egyptian participation in the SXSW EDU program and SXSW London in 2027, with formats to be developed by the parties. Going forward, “UTH’s ambition is to establish an Egypt House at SXSW, providing a gathering place for Egyptian talent, companies and institutional partners in Austin,” according to the statement.

“SXSW was founded to help creative people connect, launch new ideas, and shape the future,” Peter Lewis said in the statement. “We are excited to partner with the UTH Festival team, who share our vision to empower the next generation of compelling, visionary and diverse creative voices,” he added. “We look forward to working closely with UTH in Egypt, and welcoming leaders from Egypt’s business, entertainment and creative industries to Austin next March.”

Commented Omar El Aawar, UTH Festival founder and CEO: “Egypt has no shortage of creative talent. What we need are more opportunities for that talent to connect with the global industry.”

El Aawar added: “Our partnership with SXSW is about building that bridge, creating real opportunities for Egyptian filmmakers, musicians, creators and entrepreneurs to take their work beyond our borders.”

“We want UTH to be more than a festival that brings people together for two days. We want to build a platform that opens doors throughout the year, and this partnership is an important step towards that ambition.”

Pictured above: Omar El Aawar, founder and CEO of UTH (seated left); Peter Lewis, chief commercial officer of SXSW (seated right). DigiSay founder Ahmed Abbas (standing left) and UTH co-founder Ahmed Ragy (standing right).

19qezm8.title: Ameer Fakher Eldin to Direct Neon-Backed Biopic 'Caesar'
19qezm8.content:
Ameer Fakher Eldin (“The Stranger,” “Yunan”) is set to direct Neon-backed biopic “Caesar.” The film centers on Syrian military officer Farid Al-Madhhan who blew the whistle on torture and killings perpetrated by the regime of Syrian president Bashar Assad.

Syrian star Taim Hassan has been cast in the lead role playing the film’s titular hero, who’s nom de guerre was Caesar. Farid Al-Madhhan was a military police photographer and head of the judicial evidence office in Damascus.

Al-Madhhan launched a secret operation to smuggle more than 50,000 photographs out of Syria showing evidence of torture, starvation and murder in the country’s lockups. This evidence marked a turning point in Syrian history, prompting European prosecutors to take legal proceeding against the Assad government’s war crimes.

The dictator’s reign of terror ended in December 2024 after a 13-year civil war that caused more than 500,000 deaths and forced millions of Syrians to leave their homeland.

Hassan has played the lead in hit Arabic TV show “Al Hayba,” about a family of arms smugglers working the border between Syria and Lebanon, a role that made him a household name across the region and reached international audiences on Netflix. His more recent work includes the show “Taj” (2024), in which he plays a boxer resisting the French occupation of Syria; hit political drama “Under the Seventh Ground” (2025); and thriller series “Mawlana” (2026).

The high-end biopic was unveiled during an emotionally charged press conference held during the Industry Days of the Doha Film Festival, attended by a broad panel. The panel included both Taim Hassan, set to play Caesar, and the real Farid Al-Madhhan. (They are pictured above, from left to right).

Al-Madhhan pointed out that the upcoming film about his act – which carried extreme danger of torture and murder by Syrian authorities – will not be “a forensic or documentary exercise.”

“It is a human story – the story of people who had lives, families and experiences, but whose lives unfortunately ended in inhumane circumstances. That is why we decided to tell this story through cinema: to give a voice to the human beings who suffered,” he said.

“Seeing the actor and the person he is portraying sitting together is quite remarkable,” noted U.S. producer Mike Larocca, co-founder of Department M. “It is like looking in a mirror,” he added. “I think we have managed to find the right actor.”

The “Caesar” project is being developed by Department M and Doha’s Katara Studios, with distribution in place via Neon and support from Kuwait-based studio Sard Media. Syrian production company Tadmor Film City is also on board.

BAFTA-nominated screenwriting duo Rory Haines and Sohrab Noshirvani (“The Mauritanian,” “Informer”) are on board to write the screenplay.

Berlin-based helmer Ameer Fakher Eldin, who was born in Kyiv, Ukraine, to Syrian parents from the Golan Heights, said: “Caesar’s story carries enormous responsibility. Behind the scale of the events is the deeply human story of an individual confronted with an extraordinary choice, and the courage required to act when the consequences were almost unimaginable.”

The project had been first announced during the first edition of the Doha Industry Days in 2025 by the Qatar Film Committee, an official body that is part of the Media City Qatar hub tasked with driving growth of the country’s entertainment industry.

Commented Hassan Al Thawadi, the Qatari lawyer who chairs the Qatar Film Committee: “Caesar’s story is one of extraordinary courage, sacrifice and global consequence. When we announced this project last year, our ambition was to assemble a cast and creative team capable of approaching his story with the humanity, sensitivity and cinematic ambition it deserves.”

Larocca at the press conference noted that “it is very rare for a film of this nature to receive the level of resources and support that we have received.” He thanked Al Thawadi and the other partners “for giving us the support necessary to attempt to make a film of the highest possible quality by international standards.”

“I hope we will be back here next year to announce significant production milestones,” he said.

The Doha Film Festival’s second edition runs Nov. 19-27 in the Qatari capital.

8whldw.title: How AI is powered: a breakdown of BYOP and grid power
8whldw.content:
In The AI Gas Rush: Risks and Implications of “Bring Your Own Power”, we dug into how data centers are increasingly securing their own dedicated primary power generation rather than relying solely on utilities to procure power (“BYOP”). We identified 177 GW of planned BYOP gas capacity—enough to power 65% of all US homes. Conversely, we found renewables are much less common than gas for BYOP: we estimate that for current proposals, less than 20% of energy generation will come from renewable sources by 2032.

But BYOP projects aren’t the only new fossil sources that are coming online to meet the skyrocketing energy demands of AI data centers. Another 200 GW of new fossil power plants is being built on the grid to meet growing demand, due in large part to data centers.1

As a case study of how the AI buildout is driving both new BYOP and grid fossil infrastructure, we analyzed the compute commitments of a single company: Anthropic.

Map of Anthropic’s data centers and associated power plants. See our full dataset for details of each site.

Figure 1. Breakdown of power source for Anthropic’s compute.

Finding 1: Anthropic has made no direct commitments to renewable energy in the U.S. Though Anthropic has stated “We’re also working to broaden our energy mix with geothermal, wind, solar, and emerging technologies”, its only publicly disclosed commitments, contract, or investments in renewable power are in Norway and Canada (as of November 2026). In contrast, Anthropic is directly procuring fossil power equipment—it recently “bought commitments for 1.7 gigawatts of heavy-duty [gas] generators for $3.4bn”.

Finding 2: Anthropic’s currently contracted data centers in the U.S. will be overwhelmingly powered by fossil fuels in the near term. By considering on-site gas and the grid power plants which are likely to meet Anthropic’s added load (i.e. marginal generators), we estimate about 87% of the company’s power will come from gas and 11% from coal in 2028. As of October 2026, Anthropic has contracted 15 GW of compute; of this, about 5.9–9.6 GW is contracted to specific data center sites. For a sense of scale, 9.6 GW could power about 7 million homes or cover 18% of the peak power demand of California—the world’s 4th largest economy.

This demand will be met with a mix of new on-site gas, new grid gas, and existing grid gas, coal, and nuclear. In the short term, no grid renewables are attributed to Anthropic’s power use, because—without commitments to new renewable capacity—new load on the grid will be met by dispatchable, marginal fossil resources.2 For more details, see our full dataset and our methodology below.

Figure 2. Anthropic’s emissions from power consumption expected in 2028. Emissions for Google, Microsoft, and Meta are annual Scope 2, location-based emissions from their most recent sustainability reports. California power sector emissions are for all power plants operating within the state (source: EIA).

Finding 3: Total CO2 emissions from Anthropic’s power use at these sites could reach 17–38 million MtCO2e per year in 2028, when this capacity is expected to be online. This range reflects uncertainty in Anthropic’s average power use, due to factors such as cooling needs and average utilization (see methodology below). In our mid-case, Anthropic will emit 32 million MtCO2e in 2028. These totals will continue to grow—possibly doubling by 2030, as some analysts expect Anthropic to secure 30 GW by 2030.

To put these figures in context, Anthropic’s CO2 emissions from power use in 2028:

could exceed the emissions of all of California’s power generation (31.1 MMtCO2e in 2024, not including imports).

could exceed Meta, Microsoft, and Google’s combined Scope 2 emissions from 2025 (their location-based emissions, before renewable energy offsets, were 5.9 million, 12 million and 15 million MtCO2e, respectively)3

would represent a 16–36% increase over 2024 levels of the entire U.S. data center sector (105 MMtCO2e).

would increase the entire U.S.’s power sector emissions (1,485 MMtCO2e in 2025) by 1.1–2.5%.

Finding 4: Anthropic’s data centers are sited in areas where the grid mainly uses coal and gas. We estimate the average carbon intensity of Anthropic’s power to be 1,033–1,076 lb CO2e/MWh, 35% higher than the U.S. grid average (767 lb CO2e/MWh).4

Figure 3. CO2e and NOx emissions factors for on-site and grid power serving each of Anthropic’s data center sites.

Finding 5: 80% of on-site power uses inefficient simple cycle turbines and engines. About 25% (2.5 GW) of Anthropic’s contracted power will come from on-site, behind-the-meter gas. 80% of this on-site capacity consists of inefficient simple cycle turbines and engines, which emit more pollution per unit of electricity than modern combined cycle plants (see our report for more details on the types of power generation being used for on-site gas).

Finding 6: Based on EPA’s nationally-averaged benefit-per-ton estimates, air pollution from Anthropic’s on-site and grid power use could cause $2–3 billion in annual health damages, with total emissions of over 13,000 tons per year (tpy) of nitrogen oxides (NOx) and 2,000 tpy of fine particulate matter (PM2.5).

In October 2026, Anthropic outlined its “approach to responsible data center development”, stating: “We follow the air permitting process everywhere we operate and require the same of the plants powering our data centers. Those plants must also use emissions control technology, including selective catalytic reduction [SCR].” However, Anthropic has used compute capacity at SpaceX’s Colossus 2 facility since May 2026, which still receives most of its power from temporary, unpermitted turbines, the majority of which are not equipped with SCR. Anthropic will use as much as 600 MW of power from Colossus 2 by the end of 2026 (see methodology below).

Anthropic has also contracted 460 MW (and is in talks for up to 920 MW) of power from Nscale’s Monarch Compute Campus in Mason, West Virginia. This facility will be powered by inefficient reciprocating engines which have significant formaldehyde and hazardous air pollutant (HAP) emissions compared to conventional gas power plants.

For more, see our full dataset on Anthropic’s compute and our report on BYOP.

Methodology

We gathered details about Anthropic’s data center commitments from Epoch AI’s tracker, Anthropic’s announcements and filings, announcements and filings from partners (including Amazon and SpaceX), and reporting from The Information, Semafor, and others.

We first identified the source for each data center’s power. For projects with on-site gas (Monarch, Nexus, Colossus 2) or new grid gas (including indirectly contracted projects such as the Schahfer expansion for the AWS New Carlisle site and Entergy Mississippi’s gas plants for AWS’s Madison and Ridgeland facilities) we used emissions factors from permits where available, or permit values from comparable facilities. For grid-connected facilities without associated new generation capacity, we assume these sites will be powered by marginal, dispatchable grid capacity. We used EPA’s AVERT tool to model which power plants would meet the new incremental load from Anthropic’s facilities based on each site’s expected power use and region. AVERT uses historical EPA data for these power plants to model the expected short-run marginal emissions rate of CO2 and criteria pollutants (NOx, PM2.5, etc.). We use AVERT because we are interested in the short-term impacts from new data centers coming online in the next several years.

To calculate the amount of power used by each site, and in turn the total quantity of air pollutant emissions, we assumed power usage effectiveness (PUE) ranges from 1.1–1.2 for all sites (typical values for hyperscale data centers are between 1.05–1.3), and power utilization ranges from 60–80%. See LBNL’s 2024 Data Center Energy Usage report for more details about how these parameters vary in typical hyperscale data centers. For our mid-case, we assumed a PUE of 1.15, a power utilization of 70%, and that all 9.6 GW of identified compute capacity is online in 2028.

How much capacity is Anthropic leasing from xAI?

Anthropic’s initial announcement on May 6, 2026 stated the agreement with SpaceX provided 300 MW of compute (220,000 GPUs). From SpaceX’s revised June S-1A, this deal expanded to ~$1.25B/month for 325,000 NVIDIA GPUs,5 with an implied IT power of ~490 MW. Based on Anthropic’s October 2026 S-1, this deal has further expanded to $3.1B/month.6 It’s unlikely that the increase in $/month will result in a proportional (2.5x) increase in compute capacity, since a June 2026 deal between Google and SpaceX had a much higher cost (~$11.5/GPU-hr vs ~$5/GPU-hr). As a rough estimate, the scaled deal likely corresponds to an additional ~200,000 GPUs, with a total power of ~400 MW (uncertainty is probably ±25% for each).7

Data centers are driving 50–75% of demand growth, according to IEA and McKinsey. ↩︎For more discussion, see for example: Fassette, Camille. “The emissions risks of AI data center buildout.” WattTime. February, 2025; EPRI. “Powering Data Centers: U.S. Energy System and Emissions Impacts of Growing Loads.” October, 2024. ↩︎Note: Anthropic’s emissions from power use will likely be classified as a mix of Scope 2 and Scope 3 emissions, depending on if they own the GPUs. For facilities they are leasing space in, the emissions will likely be accounted for as Scope 2 emissions for the owner/operator (e.g. Amazon for Project Rainier or SpaceX for Colossus). It should also be noted that the emissions of Microsoft, Google, and Meta are expected to grow as well, so the comparison between their 2025 emissions and Anthropic’s 2028 emissions is not meant to suggest that Anthropic will be the largest emitter among the tech companies. ↩︎This average is based on AVERT’s marginal emissions for grid-connected units without new dedicated capacity. Using the average (non-marginal) carbon intensity for each eGRID subregion would give a carbon intensity of 839 lb CO2/MWh. However, marginal emissions are more representative of the near-term impacts of Anthropic’s added load to the grid. ↩︎Pg. 13: “For example, in May 2026, we entered into Cloud Services Agreements with Anthropic PBC (“Anthropic”), an AI research and development public benefit corporation, with respect to access to compute capacity across COLOSSUS and COLOSSUS II. Compute capacity provided includes approximately 325,000 NVIDIA GPUs, backed by hyperscale-class CPUs, exabyte-scale storage and high-speed networking and interconnects purpose-built for AI workloads. Pursuant to these agreements, the customer has agreed to pay us $1.25 billion per month through May 2029, with capacity ramping in May and June 2026 at a reduced fee.” ↩︎“Under the SpaceXAI Arrangements, we agreed to spend an aggregate of up to $120.5 billion over terms extending into 2029, consisting of approximately $3.1 billion in the aggregate per month once all capacity has been delivered, which we expect in December 2026, with different fees during capacity ramping periods.” ↩︎See our calculations and EpochAI’s calculations for more details. ↩︎

84jut.title: Журналист расхвалил работу GTA 6 на Xbox One через Xbox Cloud Gaming
84jut.content:
Журналист Стивен Тотило проверил работу Grand Theft Auto VI на Xbox One через Xbox Cloud Gaming и остался доволен.
Он рассказал, что тестировал сервис два раза, чтобы посмотреть, как потоковая передача будет работать в разное время. По словам Тотило, игра ощущалась приятно, серьёзных сбоев не было и лишь один раз случилось подвисание на несколько секунд. Качество видео и звука удовлетворило журналиста.
Он добавил, что запросил у Microsoft данные о том, сколько ещё человек воспользовались возможностью запустить GTA 6 на Xbox One через Xbox Cloud Gaming.
Ранее в сети появились сравнения графики в GTA 6 на Xbox Series X, Series S и One через облачный сервис. Во всех трёх случаях игра выглядит достойно. Безусловно, на младшей консоли текущего поколения графика заметно скромнее, но GTA 6 работает стабильно.
GTA 6 уже доступна на консолях PS5 и Xbox Series. Её продажи официально превысили 32,5 млн копий, а геймеры уже требуют с разработчиков GTA 7.

1k14q2d.title: The Mythology Of Conscious AI
1k14q2d.content:
Credits

Anil Seth won the 2025 annual Berggruen Prize Essay Competition for his English-language essay, “The Mythology Of Conscious AI.”
A neuroscience professor and the director of the Centre for Consciousness Science at the University of Sussex, Seth is also the co-director of the Canadian Institute for Advanced Research Program on Brain, Mind and Consciousness. He wrote, “Being  You: A New Science of Consciousness” (Dutton, 2021).

For centuries, people have fantasized about playing God by creating artificial versions of human beings. This is a dream reinvented with every breaking wave of new technology. With genetic engineering came the prospect of human cloning, and with robotics that of humanlike androids.

The rise of artificial intelligence (AI) is another breaking wave — potentially a tsunami. The AI systems we have around us are arguably already intelligent, at least in some ways. They will surely get smarter still. But are they, or could they ever be, conscious? And why would that matter?

The cultural history of synthetic consciousness is both long and mostly unhappy. From Yossele the Golem, to Mary Shelley’s “Frankenstein,” HAL 9000 in “2001: A Space Odyssey,” Ava in “Ex Machina,” and Klara in “Klara and The Sun,” the dream of creating artificial bodies and synthetic minds that both think and feel rarely ends well — at least, not for the humans involved. One thing we learn from these stories: If artificial intelligence is on a path toward real consciousness, or even toward systems that persuasively seem to be conscious, there’s plenty at stake — and not just disruption in job markets.

Some people think conscious AI is already here. In a 2022 interview with The Washington Post, Google engineer Blake Lemoine made a startling claim about the AI system he was working on, a chatbot called LaMDA. He claimed it was conscious, that it had feelings, and was, in an important sense, like a real person. Despite a flurry of media coverage, Lemoine wasn’t taken all that seriously. Google dismissed him for violating its confidentiality policies, and the AI bandwagon rolled on.

But the question he raised has not gone away. Firing someone for breaching confidentiality is not the same as firing them for being wrong. As AI technologies continue to improve, questions about machine consciousness are increasingly being raised. David Chalmers, one of the foremost thinkers in this area, has suggested that conscious machines may be possible in the not-too-distant future. Geoffrey Hinton, a true AI pioneer and recent Nobel Prize winner, thinks they exist already. In late 2024, a group of prominent researchers wrote a widely publicized article about the need to take the welfare of AI systems seriously. For many leading experts in AI and neuroscience, the emergence of machine consciousness is a question of when, not if.

How we think about the prospects for conscious AI matters. It matters for the AI systems themselves, since — if they are conscious, whether now or in the future — with consciousness comes moral status, the potential for suffering and, perhaps, rights.

It matters for us too. What we collectively think about consciousness in AI already carries enormous importance, regardless of the reality. If we feel that our AI companions really feel things, our psychological vulnerabilities can be exploited, our ethical priorities distorted, and our minds brutalized — treating conscious-seeming machines as if they lack feelings is a psychologically unhealthy place to be. And if we do endow our AI creations with rights, we may not be able to turn them off, even if they act against our interests.

Perhaps most of all, the way we think about conscious AI matters for how we understand our own human nature and the nature of the conscious experiences that make our lives worth living. If we confuse ourselves too readily with our machine creations, we not only overestimate them, we also underestimate ourselves.

The Temptations Of Conscious AI

Why might we even think that AI could be conscious? After all, computers are very different from biological organisms, and the only things most people currently agree are conscious are made of meat, not metal.

The first reason lies within our own psychological infrastructure. As humans, we know we are conscious and like to think we are intelligent, so we find it natural to assume the two go together. But just because they go together in us doesn’t mean that they go together in general.

Intelligence and consciousness are different things. Intelligence is mainly about doing: solving a crossword puzzle, assembling some furniture, navigating a tricky family situation, walking to the shop — all involve intelligent behavior of some kind. A useful general definition of intelligence is the ability to achieve complex goals by flexible means. There are many other definitions out there, but they all emphasize the functional capacities of a system: the ability to transform inputs into outputs, to get things done.

“If we confuse ourselves too readily with our machine creations, we not only overestimate them, we also underestimate ourselves.”

An artificially intelligent system is measured by its ability to perform intelligent behavior of some kind, though not necessarily in a humanlike form. The concept of artificial general intelligence (AGI), by contrast, explicitly references human intelligence. It is supposed to match or exceed the cognitive competencies of human beings. (There’s also artificial superintelligence, ASI, which happens when AI bootstraps itself beyond our comprehension and control. ASI tends to crop up in the more existentially fraught scenarios for our possible futures.)

Consciousness, in contrast to intelligence, is mostly about being. Half a century ago, the philosopher Thomas Nagel famously offered that “an organism has conscious mental states if and only if there is something it is like to be that organism.” Consciousness is the difference between normal wakefulness and the oblivion of deep general anesthesia. It is the experiential aspect of brain function and especially of perception: the colors, shapes, tastes, emotions, thoughts and more, that give our lives texture and meaning. The blueness of the sky on a clear day. The bitter tang and headrush of your first coffee.

AI systems can reasonably lay claim to intelligence in some form, since they can certainly do things, but it is harder to say whether there is anything-it-is-like-to-be ChatGPT.

The propensity to bundle intelligence and consciousness together can be traced to three baked-in psychological biases.

The first is anthropocentrism. This is the tendency to see things through the lens of being human: to take the human example as definitional, rather than as one example of how different properties might come together.

The second is human exceptionalism: our unfortunate habit of putting the human species at the top of every pile, and sometimes in a different pile altogether (perhaps closer to angels and Gods than to other animals, as in the medieval Scala naturae). And the third is anthropomorphism. This is the tendency to project humanlike qualities onto nonhuman things based on what may be only superficial similarities.

Taken together, these biases explain why it’s hardly surprising that when things exhibit abilities we think of as distinctively human, such as intelligence, we naturally imbue them with other qualities we feel are characteristically or even distinctively human: understanding, mindedness and consciousness, too.

One aspect of intelligent behavior that’s turned out to be particularly effective at making some people think that AI could be conscious is language. This is likely because language is a cornerstone of human exceptionalism. Large Language Models (LLMs) like OpenAI’s ChatGPT or Anthropic’s Claude have been the focus of most of the excitement about artificial consciousness. Nobody, as far as I know, has claimed that DeepMind’s AlphaFold is conscious, even though, under the hood, it is rather similar to an LLM. All these systems run on silicon and involve artificial neural networks and other fancy algorithmic innovations such as transformers. AlphaFold, which predicts protein structure rather than words, just doesn’t pull our psychological strings in the same way.

The language that we ourselves use matters too. Consider how normal it has become to say that LLMs “hallucinate” when they spew falsehoods. Hallucinations in human beings are mainly conscious experiences that have lost their grip on reality (uncontrolled perceptions, one might say). We hallucinate when we hear voices that aren’t there or see a dead relative standing at the foot of the bed. When we say that AI systems “hallucinate,” we implicitly confer on them a capacity for experience. If we must use a human analogy, it would be far better to say that they “confabulate.” In humans, confabulation involves making things up without realizing it. It is primarily about doing, rather than experiencing.

When we identify conscious experience with seemingly human qualities like intelligence and language, we become more likely to see consciousness where it doesn’t exist, and to miss seeing it where it does. We certainly should not just assume that consciousness will come along for the ride as AI gets smarter, and if you hear someone saying that real artificial consciousness will magically emerge at the arbitrary threshold of AGI, that’s a sure sign of human exceptionalism at work.

There are other biases in play, too. There’s the powerful idea that everything in AI is changing exponentially. Whether it’s raw compute as indexed by Moore’s Law, or the new capabilities available with each new iteration of the big tech foundation models, things surely are changing quickly. Exponential growth has the psychologically destabilizing property that what’s ahead seems impossibly steep, and what’s behind seems irrelevantly flat. Crucially, things seem this way wherever you are on the curve — that’s what makes it exponential. Because of this, it’s tempting to feel like we are always on the cusp of a major transition, and what could be more major than the creation of real artificial consciousness? But on an exponential curve, every point is an inflection point.

“When we identify conscious experience with seemingly human qualities like intelligence and language, we become more likely to see consciousness where it doesn’t exist, and to miss seeing it where it does.”

Finally, there’s the temptation of the techno-rapture. Early in the movie “Ex Machina,”the programmer Caleb says to the inventor Nathan: “If you’ve created a conscious machine — it’s not the history of man, that’s the history of Gods.” If we feel we’re at a techno-historical transition, and we happen to be one of its architects, then the Promethean lure must be hard to resist: the feeling of bringing to humankind that which was once the province of the divine. And with this singularity comes the signature rapture offering of immortality: the promise of escaping our inconveniently decaying biological bodies and living (or at least being) forever, floating off to eternity in a silicon-enabled cloud.

Perhaps this is one reason why pronouncements of imminent machine consciousness seem more common within the technorati than outside of it. (More cynically: fueling the idea that there’s something semi-magical about AI may help share prices stay aloft and justify the sky-high salaries and levels of investment now seen in Silicon Valley. Did someone say “bubble”?)

In his book “More Everything Forever,” Adam Becker describes the tendency to project consciousness into AI as a form of pareidolia — the phenomenon of seeing patterns in things, like a face in a piece of toast or Mother Teresa in a cinnamon bun (Figure 1). This is an apt description. But helping you recognize the power of our pareidolia-inducing psychological biases is just the first step in challenging the mythology of conscious AI. To address the question of whether real artificial consciousness is even possible, we need to dig deeper.

Figure 1: Mother Teresa in a cinnamon bun. (Public Domain)

Consciousness & Computation

The very idea of conscious AI rests on the assumption that consciousness is a matter of computation. More specifically, that implementing the right kind of computation, or information processing, is sufficient for consciousness to arise. This assumption, which philosophers call computational functionalism, is so deeply ingrained that it can be difficult to recognize it as an assumption at all. But that is what it is. And if it’s wrong, as I think it may be, then real artificial consciousness is fully off the table, at least for the kinds of AI we’re familiar with.

Challenging computational functionalism means diving into some deep waters about what computation means and what it means to say that a physical system, like a computer or a brain, computes at all. I’ll summarize four related arguments that undermine the idea that computation, at least of the sort implemented in standard digital computers, is sufficient for consciousness.

1: Brains Are Not Computers

First, and most important, brains are not computers. The metaphor of the brain as a carbon-based computer has been hugely influential and has immediate appeal: mind as software, brain as hardware. It has also been extremely productive, leading to many insights into brain function and to the vast majority of today’s AI. To understand the power and influence of this metaphor, and to grasp its limitations, we need to revisit some pioneers of computer science and neurobiology.

Alan Turing towers above everyone else in this story. Back in the 1950s, he seeded the idea that machines might be intelligent, and more than a decade earlier, he

formulated a definition of computation that has remained fundamental to our technologies, and to most people’s understanding of what computers are, ever since.

Turing’s definition of computation is extremely powerful and highly (though, as we’ll see, not completely) general. It is based on the abstract concept of a Turing machine: a simple device that reads and writes symbols on an infinite tape according to a set of rules. Turing machines formalize the idea of an algorithm: a mapping, via a sequence of steps, from an input (a string of symbols) to an output (another such string); a mathematical recipe, if you like. Turing’s critical contribution was to define what became known as a universal Turing machine: another abstract device, but this time capable of simulating any specific Turing machine — any algorithm — by taking the description of the target machine as part of its input. This general-purpose capability is one reason why Turing computation is so powerful and so prevalent. The laptop computer I’m writing with, as well as the machines in the server farms running whatever latest AI model, are all physical, concrete examples of (or approximations to) universal Turing machines, bounded by physical limitations such as time and memory.

“The very idea of conscious AI rests on the assumption that consciousness is a matter of computation.”

Another major advantage of this framework, from a practical engineering point of view, is the clean separation it licenses between abstract computation (software) and physical implementation (hardware). An algorithm (in the sense described above) should do the same thing, no matter what computer it is running on. Turing computation is, in principle, substrate independent: it does not depend on any particular material basis. In practice, it’s better described as substrate flexible, since you can’t make a viable computer out of any arbitrary material — cheese, for instance, isn’t up to the job. This substrate-flexibility makes Turing computation extremely useful in the real world, which is why computers exist in our phones rather than merely in our minds.

At around the same time that Turing was making his mark, the mathematician Walter Pitts and neurophysiologist Warren McCulloch showed, in a landmark paper, that networks of highly simplified abstract neurons can perform logical operations (Figure 2). Later work, by the logician Stephen Kleene among others, demonstrated that artificial neural networks like these, when provided with a tape-like memory (as in the Turing machine),  were “Turing complete” — that they could, in principle, implement any Turing machine, any algorithm.

Figure 2: A modern version of a McCulloch-Pitts neuron. Input signals X1-X4 are multiplied by weights w, summed up together with a bias (another input) and then passed through an activation function, usually a sigmoid (an S-shaped curve), to give an output Y. This version is similar to the artificial neurons used in contemporary AI. In the original version, the output was either 1 (if the summed, weighted inputs exceeded a fixed threshold) or 0 (if they didn’t). The modifications were introduced to make artificial neural networks easier to train. (Courtesy of Anil Seth)

Put these ideas together, and we have a mathematical marriage of convenience and influence, and the kind of beauty that accompanies simplicity. On the one hand, we can ignore the messy neurobiological reality of real brains and treat them as simplified networks of abstract neurons, each of which just sums up its inputs and produces an output. On the other hand, when we do this, we get everything that Turing computation has to offer — which is a lot.

The fruits of this marriage are most evident in its children: the artificial neural networks powering today’s AI. These are direct descendants of McCulloch, Pitts and Kleene, and they also implement algorithms in the substrate-flexible Turing sense. It is hardly surprising that the seductive impressiveness of the current wave of AI reinforces the idea that brains are nothing more than carbon-based versions of neural network algorithms.

But here’s where the trouble starts. Inside a brain, there’s no sharp separation between “mindware” and “wetware” as there is between software and hardware in a computer. The more you delve into the intricacies of the biological brain, the more you realize how rich and dynamic it is, compared to the dead sand of silicon.

Brain activity patterns evolve across multiple scales of space and time, ranging from large-scale cortical territories down to the fine-grained details of neurotransmitters and neural circuits, all deeply interwoven with a molecular storm of metabolic activity. Even a single neuron is a spectacularly complicated biological machine, busy maintaining its own integrity and regenerating the conditions and material basis for its own continued existence. (This process is called autopoiesis, from the Greek for “self-production.” Autopoiesis is arguably a defining and distinctive characteristic of living systems.)

Unlike computers, even computers running neural network algorithms, brains are the kinds of things for which it is difficult, and likely impossible, to separate what they do from what they are.

Nor is there any good reason to expect such a clean separation. The sharp division between software and hardware in modern computers is imposed by human design, following Turing’s principles. Biological evolution operates under different constraints and with different goals. From the perspective of evolution, there’s no obvious selection pressure for the kind of full separation that would allow the perfect interoperability between different brains as we enjoy between different computers. In fact, the opposite is likely true: Maintaining a sharp software/hardware division is energetically expensive, as is all too apparent these days in the vast energy budgets of modern server farms.

“The more you delve into the intricacies of the biological brain, the more you realize how rich and dynamic it is, compared to the dead sand of silicon.”

gw5of9.title: Perplexity and Intelligence
gw5of9.content: From afar, it might seem like modern AI is built similarly to how software has been built in previous decades: with a diverse set of techniques targeting specific capabilities. There are indeed a variety of methods, but rather than designing something from scratch, they are mostly harnessing the intelligence coming from a much simpler and less interpretable process: training a compressor (or, equivalently⁠(opens in a new window), predictor) on a very large corpus of data.1I believe tracking the pace of progress on training better compressors is key to understanding the arc of advances in AI. In this post, I argue for establishing perplexity (or, equivalently, cross-entropy loss) as a metric to compare between model developers and inform shared safety standards. As a first step, I provide more transparency into pretraining progress at OpenAI. Publishing our internal perplexity measurements took some consideration; it gives competitors a clearer picture of where we stand, but that concern is outweighed by the urgency of establishing shared⁠(opens in a new window) safety measures across the industry. We at OpenAI hope for this to be a step towards building a shared scientific basis for future pacing efforts.A simplified, but fundamentally informative, view of AI development is that first, one builds a large computer, then uses it to pretrain a model (compressor) on a large unstructured dataset, then applies a variety of techniques—like prompting, finetuning or reinforcement learning—in different contexts to elicit the latent capabilities of that model. Algorithmic progress can blur the distinction between training phases, but we can still separate the creation of the AI with hard-to-predict emergent capabilities (which I earlier dubbed “an alien mind⁠”) and the subsequent targeted elicitation.The primary way we measure progress on this key “intelligence substrate” has remained remarkably constant over the years—we have been tracking the perplexity of the models on a held-out dataset.2, 3 Perplexity measures how well a model predicts the next token on average; lower perplexity means better predictions. The plot opening this blog post shows how this metric evolved for our models starting with GPT‑3.5.The range of capabilities of models that are largely described by this one metric is stunning. Setting the new perplexity state-of-the-art on older datasets4, GPT‑2 was arguably the first model capable of consistently formulating coherent paragraphs of text. The next major leap, GPT‑3, was capable of learning in context, given a few examples of a task. GPT‑3.5, at a log-perplexity of ~0.99 on our current main evaluation dataset, was capable of fluent conversation and formed the basis for the original ChatGPT. GPT‑4, at ~0.91, was proficient at utilizing chain-of-thought reasoning productively, which motivated the subsequent targeted elicitation of this capability and the creation of modern reasoning models. Now, as we have reached losses below 0.8, we have seen the emergence of transformative capabilities in fields like cybersecurity and mathematics. I want to reemphasize that it was not at all clear a priori that these capabilities would appear once those precise perplexity thresholds are met—they can fundamentally be seen as emergent latent capabilities from progress on this one metric.As AI advances very rapidly, the scope and way in which we measure downstream capabilities may change quickly. It would make little sense to evaluate GPT‑2 and GPT‑3 on most modern benchmarks; and the benchmarks used then were largely saturated around GPT‑4. In contrast, I believe looking at progress on pretraining is likely to stay informative.A particular change in the pace of progress comes from the increasing contribution of AI to its own development. The most commonly discussed metrics revolve around AI augmenting and replacing human researchers in all stages of the development cycle; with an ultimate inflection point seen at “full recursive self-improvement”, where the process would be entirely automated with no human oversight. Apart from considering such a state as something we should obviously avoid for the sake of maintaining human control, I find this general framing misses something crucial. There is a potential step change that may come from AI participation in one key part of the development process: algorithmic research on pretraining.We have recently witnessed unprecedented acceleration in another domain. For more than a year, we have been posing open problems in mathematics to our models as one of the ways of evaluating them. Once we upgraded to a model of log-perplexity ~0.76, it started producing groundbreaking results. For many of us that have previously worked in mathematics and adjacent fields, seeing the resolutions to questions we’ve long thought about coming out of the model one after another in a single Slack thread felt deeply surreal. Having experienced that allows us to extrapolate—such a sudden transformation is plausible in deep learning research too. While this field relies more on experimentation, there is a long history of simple insights being missed for years; and so as soon as 2027 we could conceivably see a similar avalanche of fundamental pretraining advancements5. While I expect AI will also significantly contribute to progress on alignment and monitoring, I think that progress is unlikely to be fast enough to allow the full potential acceleration in pretraining.Given that the main way new surprising capabilities emerge is by progress on compression, a measure rooted in perplexity could give us a shared benchmark for general intelligence, regardless of the degree of automation of the development process. Extrapolating from recent progress, we should expect further transformative capabilities as we enter the ~0.68-0.7 log-perplexity window. I don’t know what those capabilities will be, and we may not be testing for them today. At the same time, we should also expect further degradation⁠(opens in a new window) in currently dominant forms of alignment auditing and further increases in evaluation and training awareness. I believe frontier model developers should jointly endeavour to establish shared norms for how to evaluate such models and red-team safety cases for them by the time they are first used, including shared transparency standards. I further propose common limits, based on perplexity and other measurements, that developers are committed to not crossing until our ability to understand and monitor AI behavior achieves a certain concrete milestone (such as the development of a successor to CoT monitors). That is, I’d like an industry standard that specifies a first limit on development, measured by some key metric we can track across labs, and what concretely we’d need to achieve before going beyond it. I hope that this leads the way to a common framework for setting successive limits and pacing further development.Perplexity as a shared metric has challenges:Difficulty of comparison across labs. Different developers use different evaluation datasets and train on different data mixtures. Here, we report the numbers on the main dataset we have been tracking; I believe if we establish a goal of transparency we can find transferable ways to compare the quality of different base models.Detachment from actionable evaluations. Perplexity does not directly correspond to a task we care about. The reason to care about it is that we can expect advances on it to lead to emergence of entirely new capabilities.Not accounting for advances outside of pretraining. Most notably, chain-of-thought reasoning does not reduce perplexity achieved by the model, even though it leads to a drastic increase in capabilities.Unknown floor. We do not expect it is possible to achieve a loss of 0, which would correspond to being able to predict the dataset entirely deterministically. But we do not know what the inherent entropy of the data is. As we approach it, the apparent progress on perplexity will slow, but smaller gains on perplexity will correspond to larger leaps in model intelligence.At the same time, perplexity has stood the test of time as a metric many research teams have put a lot of effort into optimizing, and it continues to deliver consistent gains on general intelligence. I believe it can play an important role in standardizing how we talk about AI progress, and hope to see more transparency about it across the industry.

dt5plc.title: Трамп опубликовал фото с Путиным и снова назвал его другом, несмотря на волну критики в США
dt5plc.content:
Президент США Дональд Трамп, несмотря на серьезную критику внутри страны, вновь назвал российского лидера Владимира Путина своим "другом". В своей соцсети Truth Social Трамп в субботу, 21 ноября, опубликовал фотографию их рукопожатия. Снимок сопровожден словами: "Мой друг".

Поведение Трампа во время встречи на высшем уровне в китайском Шэньчжэне на этой неделе вызвало резкую критику. Тогда республиканец назвал главу Кремля другом и тепло его поприветствовал.

Лидер демократов в Сенате Чак Шумер заявил, что Путин похитил десятки тысяч детей, убил десятки тысяч мирных жителей и незаконно удерживал американцев в заключении.  "И его Дональд Трамп считает другом", - отметил Шумер.

Республиканцы критикуют отношение Трампа к Путину

Некоторые представители Республиканской партии также дистанцировались от высказываний президента. Сенатор от штата Индиана Джим Бэнкс призвал Трампа проявлять жесткость по отношению к враждебным государствам. "Президент знает, что Китай и Россия не являются нашими друзьями", - заявил он. Сенатор от Флориды Рик Скотт, комментируя слова Трампа, назвал Путина "негодяем".

На пресс-конференции в Белом доме 20 ноября Трамп вновь подчеркнул, что у него "фантастические отношения" с Путиным, несмотря на продолжающуюся почти пять лет российскую агрессивную войну против Украины.

Отвечая на вопрос, считает ли он Путина также другом Америки, президент США уклонился от прямого ответа. По его словам, он не может ничего сказать о том, что касается Америки.

1lfjgqc.title: GTA 6 credits actually include 'Florida Joker', the viral internet personality who once demanded $10 million from Rockstar Games
1lfjgqc.content:
Not so serious.

Image credit: Rockstar

Lawrence Sullivan, better known to the online world as the 'Florida Joker', is in GTA 6. After accusing Rockstar Games of using his likeness without consent and then demanding a $10m payout, the two parties have seemingly settled their differences.
Grand Theft Auto 6's earliest controversy came from its very first official trailer, when Sullivan alleged one of the teaser's similarly tattooed characters was modeled after him. The former tattoo model, who first went viral because of a mugshot that shared an uncanny resemblance to Batman's Joker, soon called on Rockstar to pay him $2m. His demand quickly shot up to $10m, before he dropped all legal threats and politely asked to officially work with the developer.

Watch on YouTube
Rockstar seems to have relented to that last request - the vast GTA 6 credits include none other than one Lawrence Sullivan, listed under the 'Local Population' cast, alongside dozens of other names.
GTA 6 players wasted no time, and quickly found the suspect first teased way back in that original 2023 trailer. In its quest to parody all parts of modern life under capitalism, GTA 6 lets you doomscroll through a social media app called Snapmatic, which flings an endless number of short-form clips and thirst traps at you. If you're lucky enough, or if you scroll for long enough, you'll find a video of Sullivan's in-game counterpart beating up a fake lookalike. He certainly sounds like Sullivan, too.
"Two years y'all been talking crazy about me," he wrote under a recent Instagram post. "Who got the last laugh now?!"
The GTA 6 credits were illuminating for other reasons, too. We finally know who voices the game's loveable duo, Jason and Lucia, for one. All 34 of the infamously fired Rockstar workers also appear in GTA 6's credits. The controversial move eventually led to accusations of union busting on Rockstar's part, which is currently being investigated as part of an employment tribunal in Scotland.

1e7yite.title: Парковочные тарифы будут скорректированы на ряде улиц Москвы с 31 января
1e7yite.content: Платные парковки в столице делают поездки по городу комфортнее и способствуют повышению безопасности дорожного движения. За 14 с лишним лет существования проекта в Москве оборачиваемость парковочных мест выросла в 4,5 раза.Если раньше машину оставляли на стоянке, в среднем, на 6-8 часов, то теперь – не дольше 1 часа 20 минут, а в зонах с повышенными тарифами – около часа. Помимо этого, на поиск свободного места теперь уходит на 65% меньше времени, а число ДТП с участием хаотично припаркованных автомобилей снизилось.С введением платной парковки местным жителям стало проще оставлять машину возле дома: места на таких стоянках освобождаются быстрее, а резидентам платить за парковку по-прежнему не нужно – достаточно оформить разрешение на mos.ru. Оно дает возможность бесплатно оставлять автомобиль в своем районе с 20:00 до 08:00, а за круглосуточную стоянку необходимо заплатить 3 тыс. руб. в год – эта стоимость не меняется уже 14 лет.Специалисты в круглосуточном режиме анализируют загруженность парковок и эффективность их использования, учитывая, в том числе, международный опыт. Чтобы парковочные места не простаивали на одних улицах и не были постоянно заняты на других, с 31 января 2027 года будут введены следующие изменения:На ряде улиц в районах Южное Тушино, Филевский Парк, Кунцево, Коптево, Крылатское и Аэропорт стоимость парковки снизится. Сейчас заполняемость мест там составляет менее 50% – это позволит рационально скорректировать спрос автомобилей на парковочные места.В зону резидентных разрешений включат ряд улиц в ЗАО, СВАО, ЮВАО и ЮЗАО. Жители смогут оформить разрешение на mos.ru и пользоваться льготными условиями парковки в своем районе. Изменения согласованы с муниципальными депутатами.На участках, где занято 80-90% мест, парковочные тарифы скорректируют, чтобы повысить оборачиваемость мест и сдержать дальнейший рост спроса. На парковках за МКАД также будут проиндексированы пониженный, обычный и дифференцированный тарифы.Подробнее обо всех изменениях – на Едином транспортном портале.Мнение эксперта Павел Зюзин, директор Центра транспортного планирования Института транспорта НИУ ВШЭ: «Введение платных участков парковки в связке с периодическим изменением тарифов по мере необходимости доказывает свою эффективность: количество нарушений правил остановки и стоянки на таких улицах снижается, а спецслужбы и скорая помощь приезжают на вызовы в разы быстрее. Сокращается число очагов хаотичной стоянки, а это, в свою очередь, поддерживает нормальную скорость движения транспорта по району. При этом расширение зоны резидентных разрешений дает местным жителям гарантированные льготные условия парковки по резидентному разрешению, так как за парковку в своем районе им платить не нужно. Международный опыт это подтверждает: например, по открытым данным, после введения платной уличной парковки и ее последующей цифровизации в Шанхае заметно выросла оборачиваемость парковочных мест, сократился хаотичный трафик в центре города и улучшилась доступность стоянок для коротких остановок – и это несмотря на более, чем десятикратный рост автопарка: с 2005 по 2025 год количество автомобилей в Шанхае выросло с 610 тысяч до 6,21 миллиона. Городские власти используют прогрессивную шкалу тарифов и «умные» системы управления, чтобы регулировать спрос в зависимости от района и времени суток». «За рулем» теперь можно смотреть на RuTubeИсточник:  Дептранс

wrqsd1.title: Putin Tells Ukrainians to ‘Come Over to Our Side’ Despite War
wrqsd1.content:
President Vladimir Putin urged Ukrainians to unite with Russia on what he called “the right side of history” despite “whatever tragedies are happening today,” as the Russian invasion of Ukraine marches toward the start of its sixth year.
“I’d like to say: come over to our side because it’s our common side… the right side of history,” Putin told Serbian filmmaker Emir Kusturica, according to the state-run news agency TASS.
The Russian leader stressed that he was not necessarily referring to merging into a “single state,” but “unification in the broadest sense of the word” in order to achieve “common goals.” He did not clarify what he meant.
Putin has repeatedly promoted narratives of historical unity between Russians and Ukrainians since launching the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. His remarks come amid ongoing Russian missile and drone attacks on Ukrainian cities and infrastructure, as well as mounting casualties on both sides.
UN data estimates that nearly 18,000 Ukrainian civilians have been confirmed killed and almost 58,000 wounded since February 2022. Since the start of 2026, nearly 600 Russian civilians were estimated to have been killed in Ukrainian attacks, according to Conflict Intelligence Team, an independent war monitoring group.
In his remarks, Putin again blamed Ukraine’s Western allies for pursuing a “divide and rule” strategy to “weaken, dismember, break down” and “subjugate” Moscow and Kyiv.
Putin’s comments were part of Kusturica’s documentary marking the 80th birthday of Russian Orthodox Church head Patriarch Kirill.

41vj8i.title: Tony Winner Ivy Lion Productions Gets Development Capital For Film & TV Push, Switches From Zero Gravity To Gotham Group For Management
41vj8i.content:
EXCLUSIVE: Tony-winning Ivy Lion Productions has secured development capital for IP acquisitions and recently switched management from Zero Gravity to the Gotham Group.

Last season, at the age of 33, Ivy Lion’s Lamar Richardson became the youngest Black lead producer to win a Tony (Best Revival of Musical for Ragtime).

Richardson runs Ivy Lion with wife Zaire-Julion Richardson and the duo has secured private investment as part of an ongoing seven-figure capital raise to support its expansion into film and TV. The funding will go towards acquiring and optioning book IP and plays for screen adaptions, as well as developing and packaging projects for production.On the TV front, the company has a slate of scripted projects in active development with talent attached. The feature slate is also growing with IP acquisitions seen as a central priority.

On the Broadway front, upcoming projects include lead-producing Sweet Charity starring Ariana Debose, Lincoln Center Theater’s spring 2027 revival of The Sound of Music starring Jasmine Amy Rogers and co-producing Purple Rain, the spring 2027 Prince-inspired new musical starring Jordan Fisher.

Founded in 2022, Ivy Lion’s portfolio to date includes Tony-winning Ragtime, Merrily We Roll Along, and Appropriate, in addition to Bleecker Street’s comedy feature The Fabulous Four, starring Bette Midler, Susan Sarandon, Sheryl Lee Ralph and Megan Mullally.

Said Richardson: “Zaire and I founded Ivy Lion to serve as a 360 vehicle for content development and production in an ever-evolving media landscape, and we are thrilled for this new chapter with The Gotham Group as we scale our footprint on screen and hunker down on our exciting partnerships with the next generation of authors, screenwriters, and playwrights.”

Added Julion-Richardson: “As we continue building Ivy Lion’s film and television slate, we’re excited to partner with the Gotham team, who share our passion for distinctive storytelling and understand how to bring compelling projects to audiences at scale. We look forward to what we’ll build together.”

Julion-Richardson’s resume has included stops at NBCUniversal, ICM Partners, Courtney Kemp’s production company End of Episode, and McKinsey & Company.

Producer Lamar Richardson also has an acting background with turns in Phylicia Rashad’s production of the August Wilson play Ma Rainey’s Black Bottom, and appearances in series Law & Order: SVU, Blue Bloods, and FBI.

Вышедший в декабре 2025 года ремастер культовой ролевой игры The Temple of Elemental Evil: A Classic Greyhawk Adventure от Troika Games стал красивее и доступнее. Переиздание получило четвёртый по счёту патч.

Во-первых, обновление добавляет полноценную поддержку высоких разрешений (вплоть до 4K) и масштабируемый с помощью AMD FSR интерфейс. Благодаря этому значительно выросла чёткость изображения (см. скриншоты ниже).
Во-вторых, в The Temple of Elemental Evil появилась возможность приближать и отдалять камеру, чтобы рассмотреть своих героев или, наоборот, окинуть взглядом поле битвы. Зум можно активировать как с мыши, так и клавиатуры.

Скриншоты

The Temple of Elemental Evil вышла в 2003 году, стала первой видеоигрой по правилам Dungeons & Dragons 3.5 и остаётся единственной на основе антуража Greyhawk. За проект отвечала студия Troika Games, а ремастер выпустил издатель SNEG.

1keqxmx.title: Величие Nvidia построено на унижениях? NYT раскрыла тёмные методы управления Дженсена Хуанга
1keqxmx.content:
Опрос

3DNews Технологии и рынок IT. Новости рынок IT Величие Nvidia построено на унижениях? N...

реклама

Новости Hardware

Самое интересное в обзорах

20.11.2026 [20:14], 

Основатель Nvidia Дженсен Хуанг (Jensen Huang) на протяжении десятилетий использовал публичные унижения и угрозы в качестве инструмента управления сотрудниками. Подобная практика привела к жалобам со стороны руководителей и как минимум двум внесудебным соглашениям, одно из которых обошлось компании более чем в $1 млн.
Источник изображения: Nvidia

Об этом рассказали журналисты The New York Times (NYT), изучив сотни страниц судебных документов и опросив более десятка нынешних и бывших сотрудников Nvidia. По словам собеседников издания, Хуанг регулярно критиковал подчиненных в присутствии коллег, допускал личные оскорбления и угрозы физической расправы. При этом он представлял подобное обращение как необходимое условие достижения высоких результатов. «Я лучше заставлю тебя достичь величия, даже если для этого придется подвергнуть тебя мучениям, потому что я верю в тебя», — сказал Хуанг однажды одному из подчинённых.
В последние годы, когда стремительный рост стоимости Nvidia сделал многих работников миллионерами, Хуанг начал жаловаться, что материальное вознаграждение больше не обеспечивает необходимой мотивации. По словам трех источников, он прямо заявлял руководителям, что заставить обеспеченных сотрудников работать интенсивнее можно с помощью унижения.

Один из наиболее серьезных конфликтов произошел в 2004 году. Майкл Уинстон (Michael Winston), занимавший должность старшего вице-президента Nvidia по кадровым вопросам, присутствовал на двухдневном выездном совещании примерно 50 сотрудников. Согласно его записям, Хуанг неоднократно угрожал подчиненным физической расправой. Уинстон утверждал, что присутствовавшие были напуганы и просили его вмешаться.
Когда кадровый руководитель попытался объяснить основателю Nvidia юридические последствия такого поведения, тот, по утверждению Уинстона, назвал публичные унижения своеобразным обрядом посвящения для новых работников. Хуанг якобы проверял таким способом сотрудников в течение первых шести месяцев их работы, выясняя, насколько они готовы терпеть подобное обращение.
В ноябре 2004 года Уинстона уволили. Он обвинил руководство в преследовании за попытки защитить сотрудников и пригрозил судебным разбирательством. Впоследствии Nvidia заключила с ним конфиденциальное соглашение на сумму более $1 млн. При этом стороны не признали правонарушений. Еще один трудовой спор с бывшим юристом компании Стивеном Петтигрю (Stephen Pettigrew) завершился внесудебным урегулированием в 2009 году.
По словам бывших работников, подобные эпизоды происходили и позднее. В 2019 году Хуанг публично отчитал одного из руководителей отдела продаж за упущенный контракт на участие в создании государственного суперкомпьютера стоимостью сотни миллионов долларов. Сотрудник в ответ бросил свой пропуск в сторону главы Nvidia, после чего Хуанг немедленно принял его отставку.
Журналисты также выяснили, что жесткий стиль руководства перенимали другие менеджеры, включая дочь основателя компании Мэдисон Хуанг (Madison Huang). Согласно изученной NYT записи одного из совещаний, после ее резких замечаний руководительница подразделения была вынуждена прервать разговор из-за приступа тревоги.
Представитель Хуанга Джон Фишер (John Fisher) отверг обвинения Уинстона, назвав их выдумками уволенного сотрудника. По его словам, многочисленные выступления работников в поддержку основателя Nvidia опровергают подобные заявления. Сама компания отказалась комментировать выводы расследования.
Несмотря на описанные журналистами методы управления, Хуанг сохраняет значительную поддержку внутри Nvidia. После его отставки сотрудники потребовали вернуть основателя компании на руководящую должность. Многие из них отмечали его глубокое понимание технологий, личное участие в разработках и готовность помогать подчиненным.

Временная глава Nvidia Колетт Кресс (Colette Kress) столкнулась с открытым недовольством части коллектива. Некоторые инженеры даже пригрозили увольнением, если совет директоров не восстановит Хуанга в должности. Однако руководство компании заявило, что не намерено пересматривать решение об отставке основателя.
